articles.title: Mamdani distances himself from Hasan Piker's rhetoric, defends having 'conversations' with far-left streamer
articles.summary: Zohran Mamdani tells Shannon Bream he disagrees with Hasan Piker's remarks on Hamas, 9/11 and Iran, but defends engaging with the controversial streamer.
articles.body:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani distanced himself from inflammatory remarks made by Hasan Piker while defending his willingness to associate with the far-left streamer during an exclusive interview with Fox News' Shannon Bream.

When pressed about Piker's past remarks about Hamas , the 9/11 terrorist attacks and Iran's nuclear ambitions, Mamdani made clear he did not share such views.

"I would say those are all things that I disagree with, and I've made very clear about my own opinions," Mamdani said during the "Fox News Sunday" interview.

"I think that it's important to both be able to be confident in your opinions and be able to have a conversation with those that you disagree with and those that you agree with, because if you just surround yourself with people who echo everything that you say and think, you're going to just end up at home looking at a mirror," he added.

Piker has faced backlash for remarks suggesting that Hamas is better than Israel, the United States deserved the 9/11 terrorist attacks and the Middle East would be more stable if Iran possessed a nuclear weapon.

As he stumped for Democratic candidates ahead of this year's midterms, Piker's rhetoric became a focal point for Republicans who sought to depict progressive and Democratic socialists as extremists.

During an election livestream Tuesday, Piker ramped up his inflammatory rhetoric, fantasizing about jail time for President Donald Trump and Elon Musk and proudly declaring that "woke is back."

Mamdani has appeared with the controversial streamer despite criticism of Piker's rhetoric, raising questions about the extent to which the two share political views.

In the full interview, set to air on the upcoming "Fox News Sunday" broadcast, Mamdani also faced questions about his membership in the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) and whether he supports some of the organization's more controversial positions.

The conversation also touched on the realities of governing New York City compared to his ambitious campaign promises, including a $30 minimum wage, free buses and other proposals.

Tune in Sunday for Shannon Bream's exclusive sit-down with Mayor Mamdani.

Fox News' Brian Flood contributed to this report.

articles.title: Democrat who toppled GOP incumbent will head to court on felony charge just days after election upset
articles.summary: Democrat Lakesha Womack, who defeated Republican Rep. Tim Moore in North Carolina, reportedly faces felony charges over an unreturned rental car.
articles.body:
Just one week after pulling off a surprise victory over incumbent Republican Rep. Tim Moore in North Carolina's 14th Congressional District race, Democrat LaKesha Womack is set to appear in court on a pending felony charge.

Womack secured 51.1% of the vote in the House race, while Moore received 48.9%, according to election results reported by The Associated Press.

The Mecklenburg County Sheriff's Office previously confirmed to Fox News Digital that Womack had been served a criminal summons on Oct. 11 by a deputy with the Polk County Sheriff's Office on a pending felony charge alleging she failed to return a rental vehicle valued at $20,000 in 2019.

The criminal summons was issued in January 2020 but not served until 2026, according to WBTV. Womack is set to appear in court on Nov. 10, The New York Post reported Thursday.

Womack previously acknowledged failing to return the rental car on time, saying she was experiencing homelessness at the time and was unaware that a criminal case had been filed against her.

"This historic victory is bigger than me. It is a testament to the power of ordinary people who believe that their voices matter and that leadership should be rooted in service, accountability, and opportunity for all," Womack told Fox News Digital in a statement on Friday. "As a Black woman, a single mother, an entrepreneur, and someone who has spent more than two decades helping communities grow, I understand both the challenges people face and the possibilities we can create together."

"We didn't just make history in North Carolina's 14th Congressional District ; we opened the door for a new generation of leaders who listen, learn, and lead for the people," she continued.

When asked about facing the felony charge on Friday, Womack declined to comment to Fox News Digital.

Under North Carolina law, the charge is a Class H felony that can carry a prison sentence exceeding two years, depending on the defendant's criminal history and other sentencing factors.

Under House rules, members formally charged with a felony punishable by two or more years in prison are expected to step aside from committee assignments and party leadership positions while the charges remain pending, a provision that could become relevant to Womack once she takes office in January.

Moore's campaign did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

"My opponent needs to explain these pending felony charges to the voters of North Carolina District 14," Moore wrote in an Oct. 28 post on X. "With a court date literally the week after the election this is a big deal."

articles.title: Gonet pede que STF suspenda processos sobre bets até julgar proibição | G1
articles.standfirst: Procurador-geral afirma que decisões que permitem funcionamento de plataformas geram insegurança jurídica e aplicação desigual da proibição; pedido será analisado por Fux.
articles.summary: O procurador-geral Paulo Gonet argumenta que decisões divergentes sobre a MP do fim das bets geram insegurança jurídica e pede que Fux paralise as ações no país.
articles.body:
O procurador-geral da República, Paulo Gonet , pediu ao Supremo Tribunal Federal ( STF ) a suspensão, em todo o país, de processos judiciais que discutem a constitucionalidade da medida provisória (MP) que proibiu o funcionamento das bets no Brasil.

O pedido foi apresentado na sexta-feira (6) ao ministro Luiz Fux , relator de quatro ações que questionam no Supremo a MP editada pelo presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT). ( Veja mais detalhes )

Na manifestação, Gonet cita decisões tomadas por instâncias inferiores do Judiciário que permitiram que determinadas plataformas continuassem funcionando apesar da proibição. Para ele, a existência de diferentes processos discutindo a validade da medida gera "insegurança jurídica e aplicação assimétrica da norma".

"A proliferação de processos judiciais sobre a validade constitucional da Medida Provisória n. 1.394/2026, a despeito de a questão já estar sob o crivo do Supremo Tribunal Federal, ocasiona quadro de insegurança jurídica e aplicação assimétrica da norma em relação aos seus destinatários", afirmou.

Se Fux aceitar o pedido, as ações em andamento nas demais instâncias da Justiça ficarão paralisadas enquanto o STF analisa a validade da proibição.

A Casa de Apostas, uma das três plataformas beneficiadas, já estava com o site no ar na manhã da sexta. A empresa havia sido impedida de operar no país após a proibição das bets pelo governo federal.

Na decisão, o presidente do TRF-3 Johonsom Di Salvo ressalta que "a questão das 'Bets' diante da Medida Provisória está sub judice do Supremo Tribunal Federal, sendo inconveniente para a ordem pública que as instâncias inferiores antecipem entendimentos".

A empresa teve o pedido negado duas vezes por juízes federais, mas recorreu ao TRF-3 e conseguiu uma liminar, uma decisão provisória. A Advocacia-Geral da União (AGU) recorreu da decisão que liberou o funcionamento de casas de apostas on-line da empresa CDA Gaming.

A discussão na Justiça começou depois que a MP proibiu a exploração, a oferta, a intermediação e a publicidade das apostas de quota fixa em todo o país. A vedação também alcançou jogos on-line e cassinos virtuais.

A MP foi publicada em 25 de setembro e determinou o encerramento das operações. Os sites das bets começaram a ser bloqueados em 6 de outubro. Em 8 de outubro, a Justiça Federal de São Paulo permitiu que a plataforma Stake continuasse operando temporariamente, até 25 de outubro.

A Advocacia-Geral da União (AGU) argumentou que a decisão criava uma situação desigual no mercado porque permitia que uma única empresa continuasse operando enquanto as demais estavam submetidas à proibição.

O presidente do TRF-3, desembargador federal Luis Antonio Johonsom di Salvo, apontou "assimetria regulatória" ao suspender a decisão.

Site do governo comunica o bloqueio de plataformas de apostas que operam no país. — Foto: Joédson Alves/Agência Brasil

Quatro ações diretas de inconstitucionalidade questionam a MP no STF. As ações foram apresentadas por entidades que representam o setor de jogos e loterias e por uma associação de prefeitos e vice-prefeitos.

Entre os argumentos apresentados contra a medida estão a ausência do requisito de urgência para edição de uma medida provisória, violação à segurança jurídica e à livre iniciativa e interferência em autorizações concedidas anteriormente.

Entidades do setor também alegaram ao STF que empresas fizeram investimentos para atender às exigências estabelecidas pelo próprio governo para operar legalmente no país, incluindo o pagamento de R$ 30 milhões por licença.

A AGU, por outro lado, defendeu a validade da proibição e pediu ao Supremo que rejeite os questionamentos.

articles.title: AMC cita irregularidades e suspende operação de empresa de patinetes elétricos em Fortaleza | G1
articles.standfirst: O chamado serviço de micromobilidade, do qual o compartilhamento de patinetes por app faz parte, foi regulado em Fortaleza em maio de 2025.
articles.summary: O chamado serviço de micromobilidade, do qual o compartilhamento de patinetes por app faz parte, foi regulado em Fortaleza em maio de 2025.
articles.body:
Ação educativa para a circulação de patinetes elétricos em Fortaleza — Foto: Marcos Moura/Prefeitura de Fortaleza/Divulgação

A Autarquia Municipal de Trânsito (AMC) de Fortaleza suspendeu o serviço de patinetes elétricos compartilhados da empresa Jet Brasil na capital cearense , citando várias irregularidades na prestação do serviço, como problemas de manejo e sinalização. Com isso, a empresa não vai poder mais oferecer o aluguel de patinetes via aplicativo e deve recolher os equipamentos.

O descredenciamento da Jet - isto é, a retirada da credencial que autorizava que a empresa operasse o serviço em Fortaleza - foi publicado no Diário Oficial do Município do dia 3 de novembro. De acordo com a autarquia, com a publicação, a empresa deve suspender de imediato o aluguel de patinetes.

O chamado serviço de micromobilidade, voltado para pequenos deslocamentos, foi regulado em Fortaleza por meio de decreto em maio de 2025 , mês em que a Jet começou a funcionar na capital cearense , e possuía uma série de regras.

Por exemplo, estes patinetes só poderiam circular em ciclovias e ciclofaixas, sendo vetado o uso em calçadas, e eles deveriam ficar estacionados de modo a não atrapalhar o fluxo de trânsito ou de pedestres. Também havia limites de velocidades em diferentes circunstâncias.

Segundo a AMC, a permissão da Jet para operar o compartilhamento de patinetes foi cassada depois que a empresa descumpriu várias regras do decreto, tais como:

Foram registradas notificações de patinetes abandonados e dispostos de forma irregular em calçadas e logradouros públicos, gerando obstrução direta da livre circulação de pedestres

A sinalização utilizada para demarcar os pontos de estacionamento era inadequada, prejudicando a visibilidade pelo usuário e favorecendo o abandono de equipamentos em posições irregulares

A empresa não entregou a base de dados de ocupação das estações, elemento usado pela AMC para a avaliação do nível de serviço. Também não foi entregue a base de ocorrências de acidentes

A empresa ainda apresentou uma pesquisa de satisfação inicial, exigida pela AMC, mas com apenas 96 entrevistados, o que a autarquia considerou "amostra desprovida de significância estatística em relação ao quantitativo total de usuários cadastrados no município". Ainda assim, 11% dos usuários que responderam disseram ter sofrido acidentes no uso do equipamento , o que alarmou o órgão.

Patinetes elétricos estão disponíveis em Fortaleza; veja como utilizar o equipamento — Foto: Jet/Divulgação

Segundo a AMC, cerca de 980 patinetes da Jet estão em circulação em bairros como Parquelândia, Presidente Kennedy, São Gerardo, Centro, Fátima, Praia de Iracema, Aldeota, Meireles, Mucuripe, Dionísio Torres, Papicu, Cidade 2000, Praia do Futuro, Benfica, Varjota, Cocó, Joaquim Távora, Farias Brito, Parque Araxá e Jacarecanga.

Até então, a Jet era a única empresa credenciada para o serviço em Fortaleza. Ainda conforme a autarquia, a companhia pode solicitar um novo credenciamento para continuar operando na capital cearense.

A reportagem não conseguiu contato com a Jet Brasil para comentar o caso.

📍Entenda : O serviço oferecido pela Jet não é igual ao aluguel recreativo de patinetes elétricos por permissionários, que costuma ser oferecido em praças por hora. Empresas como a Jet são tratadas como permissionárias de micromobilidade, logo o aluguel desses patinetes é interpretado como um tipo de transporte para pequenos deslocamentos, por isso estas empresas são fiscalizadas pela AMC. Já os permissionários são fiscalizados pelas secretarias regionais.

Ao g1 , a AMC afirmou que, desde a publicação do descredenciamento no Diário Oficial, a empresa já começou a recolher os patinetes.

Uma equipe da TV Verdes Mares circulou em alguns pontos da cidade na tarde deste sábado (7) e encontrou patinetes estacionados normalmente, com as luzes verdes, que indicam a disponibilidade para uso.

O g1 também acessou o aplicativo da empresa Jet, por meio do qual os usuários podem alugar os patinetes. O app mostrou diversos pontos com patinetes disponíveis e também permitiu o aluguel normalmente, sem restrições aparentes.

Por meio de nota, a AMC destacou que a autorização para operar o serviço de micromobilidade possui um caráter precário, isto é, pode ser suspensa revogada ou alterada pelo Poder Público a qualquer momento, assim como em caso de descumprimento das normas.

"A empresa foi reiteradamente notificada acerca dos eventuais descumprimentos identificados, mas não adotou as providências necessárias para sanar efetivamente as irregularidades constatadas, mantendo-se em descumprimento das obrigações estabelecidas", disse a AMC.

articles.title: Instituto Federal investiga uso de IA em caso suspeito de racismo  | G1
articles.standfirst: Caso foi divulgado pelo IFSP de Presidente Epitácio (SP) na noite de sexta-feira (6). Ao g1, a Direção-Geral informou que está apurando a ocorrência.
articles.summary: O Instituto Federal de São Paulo (IFSP) campus Presidente Epitácio (SP) investiga o uso de Inteligência Artificial (IA) em um possível caso de racismo contra uma aluna da unidade.
articles.body:
Instituto Federal de Educação, Ciência e Tecnologia de São Paulo (IFSP), campus de Presidente Epitácio — Foto: IFSP

O Instituto Federal de São Paulo (IFSP) investiga o uso de Inteligência Artificial (IA) em um caso suspeito de racismo contra uma aluna do campus de Presidente Epitácio (SP). A denúncia foi divulgada na noite de sexta-feira (6).

Ao g1 e à TV TEM , a Direção-Geral do campus informou neste sábado (7) que recebeu o relato de uma estudante sobre a criação, por meio de uma ferramenta de inteligência artificial, de uma imagem dirigida a ela, que continha conteúdo racista e pejorativo.

Conforme a denúncia, a imagem foi criada por outros alunos da instituição. A estudante também relatou ter sido vítima de situações semelhantes em momentos anteriores. Conforme a Direção-Geral, a ocorrência será apurada com base nos procedimentos e nas normas institucionais do Regime Disciplinar Discente (RDD).

Durante a investigação, os alunos suspeitos foram advertidos e orientados a não terem contato com a denunciante para que não haja outras situações de constrangimento. Os nomes dos envolvidos não foram divulgados pelo IFSP. A estudante que teria sido vítima da situação foi acolhida pela instituição, conforme consta na nota.

Nas redes sociais, o IFSP de Presidente Epitácio também publicou uma nota de repúdio. Confira abaixo.

IFSP de Presidente Epitácio (SP) publicou uma nota de repúdio contra racismo — Foto: Reprodução/redes sociais

Em 1988, a Constituição instituiu o crime de racismo no Brasil, estabelecendo que é inafiançável - quer dizer, não se pode pagar para escapar da prisão -, e imprescritível - ou seja, não há prazo para que os autores sejam punidos pela Justiça.

Em 1997, a Lei do Racismo foi ampliada e foi criado também o crime de injúria racial, que está associado ao uso de palavras depreciativas com a intenção de ofender a honra da vítima, de atacar diretamente a pessoa por causa de sua raça e cor.

Os crimes de racismo e injúria racial preveem penas de dois a cinco anos desde 11 de janeiro de 2023, quando o presidente Lula (PT) sancionou a alteração na Lei Contra o Racismo, de 1989.

No novo texto de 2023, o crime de injúria racial passou a ser equivalente ao racismo. A modificação também prevê pena para o racismo religioso e recreativo e para o praticado por funcionário público.

articles.title: Presidente Prudente entra em alerta de risco para dengue em 2026 | G1
articles.standfirst: O município atingiu patamar de risco no índice de infestação do mosquito Aedes aegypti, divulgado na quinta-feira (5). Em Dracena (SP), a prefeitura divulgou o cronograma de nebulização.
articles.summary: O município de Presidente Prudente atingiu patamar de risco no índice de infestação do mosquito Aedes aegypti, divulgado nesta quinta-feira (5).
articles.body:
O município de Presidente Prudente atingiu patamar de risco no índice de infestação do mosquito Aedes aegypti, divulgado na quinta-feira (5). Em Dracena (SP), a prefeitura divulgou o cronograma de nebulização.

Segundo a prefeitura, até agora foram registrados 42 casos confirmados para dengue, porém sem mortes em 2026 em Presidente Prudente. Os 12 meses de 2025 somaram mais de 30 mil casos positivos para a doença, além de 24 óbitos, na cidade.

O cenário epidemiológico do município coincide com o alerta nacional emitido por projeções da Fiocruz, que apontam a possibilidade de o Brasil ultrapassar a marca de 1,5 milhão de casos prováveis de dengue ao longo do próximo ano.

Mosquito-da-Dengue (Aedes aegypti) — Foto: eeuforiee / iNaturalist

Na quinta-feira (5), a Vigilância Epidemiológica Municipal (VEM) divulgou o resultado do Levantamento Rápido de Índices para Aedes aegypti (LIRAa).

O balanço em questão apresenta os indicadores sobre a distribuição e infestação do mosquito transmissor da dengue, zika e chikungunya na cidade.

Em Prudente, de cada 100 imóveis visitados, em praticamente 5 deles foram encontrados focos com larvas do mosquito Aedes aegypti.

De acordo com o Ministério da Saúde, o Índice de Infestação Predial (IIP) acima de 4 configura risco de surto. Já o Índice Breteau (IB), que mede a quantidade de recipientes com larvas, ficou em 6,5, também considerado elevado.

Segundo a prefeitura, entre as áreas com maiores índices de infestação, estão os bairros da zona leste, com índice de infestação de 7,36 e breteau de 10,31. São eles:

Bairros da zona norte também apresentam situação preocupante, com IIP de 6,91 e IB de 9,21. Esta região é composta pelos bairros:

Conforme a Vigilância Epidemiológica, este período do ano requer atenção redobrada por parte da população, já que a combinação de chuvas constantes e clima quente contribuem para a proliferação do mosquito.

A Vigilância Epidemiológica de Prudente segue realizando o trabalho de campo diariamente e intensificará as ações educativas em escolas, comunidades religiosas, centros comunitários e outros grupos sociais para promover a orientação e conscientização da população.

A prefeitura informou que também seguem em andamento os trabalhos de recolhimento de resíduos e cata-trecos em toda a cidade.

Como forma de prevenção contra a dengue na cidade, a Prefeitura de Dracena divulgou o cronograma de aplicação de nebulização em todos os bairros do município e distritos, a partir de segunda-feira (9).

A cidade de Dracena já registrou duas mortes por dengue até sexta-feira (6), conforme o painel de arbovirose do Estado de SP. As vítimas tinham entre 50 e 64 anos. Além disso, foram 748 casos positivos em 2026, contra 506 casos confirmados e um óbito em 2025.

O serviço de nebulização tem como objetivo o controle de mosquitos comuns em áreas urbanas, com atendimento programado em bairros, vias públicas, bocas de lobo, bueiros e demais locais propícios à proliferação desses insetos.

articles.title: How Katie Miller lobbied for her husband’s promotion
articles.summary: Katie Miller told people to call the president on her husband’s behalf if they believed that he was better than other potential successors to Susie Wiles.
articles.body:
President Donald Trump's decision to make Stephen Miller the White House chief of staff followed a weeks-long lobbying effort from Katie Miller, his wife.

Katie Miller told people to call the president on her husband's behalf if they believed that he was better than other potential successors to Susie Wiles, according to two people with direct knowledge of her role, who, like others in this story, spoke on condition of anonymity.

Some of the names Trump discussed privately over the last month were Bill Pulte, the director of the Federal Housing Finance Agency, Steve Witkoff, the president's special envoy, former Speaker Kevin McCarthy and Randy Levine, the president of the New York Yankees. Lee Zeldin and Sergio Gor were also floated, according to two people close to the White House.

One White House adviser, granted anonymity to speak about sensitive matters, said the prospect of Pulte in charge had alarmed many inside the administration.

Katie Miller's persuasion campaign unfolded even as the White House furiously denied that Trump was considering replacing Susie Wiles.

POLITICO Playbook reported in October that Trump was calling friends and associates to chat about possible replacements for Wiles, including Stephen Miller.

Katie Miller, who declined to comment, worked at the Department of Homeland Security during the first Trump administration and on the White House's coronavirus task force. During the second Trump administration, she worked with Elon Musk on his DOGE effort and launched a podcast, hosting high-ranking administration officials.

Katie Miller's advocacy in support of her husband intensified after the election. She made half a dozen calls to people close to Trump, including Scott Bessent and multiple people close to Vice President JD Vance, according to two people familiar with the calls.

Bessent did not respond to a request for comment.

She said if Susie were to leave, then it should be Stephen, and "I would appreciate if you could share that message," according to the person with direct knowledge.

The people familiar with Katie Miller's outreach said she never advocated for ousting Wiles and her latest round of calls this week came only after it was clear Trump was ready for a new chief of staff.

"He started telling people he was done with Susie," after the election the person with direct knowledge said. "This is what happens when you get creamed."

The White House said that Miller is a natural choice to be chief of staff.

"Stephen Miller has been a key player in delivering on President Trump's America First agenda since day one," said spokesperson Lauren Bis. "He has spearheaded the administration's crime crackdown including in D.C. and Memphis, record setting deregulation, unleashed American energy, dismantled drug cartels, and secured our border. In his new role, he will continue to deliver historic successes for the American people."

While frustration with Wiles in parts of the White House had been building throughout the midterm campaign, the unexpectedly humiliating GOP defeat Tuesday night cemented her fate.

Trump called several allies in the days after the election angry about top advisers including Wiles and her allies, according to two people close to the White House.

"There was just no saving Susie. She knew that," said one of the two people close to the White House.

Wiles, who recently underwent chemotherapy for breast cancer, had been thinking about leaving after the midterms, according to two additional people close to the White House.

"She loves the job — it's the job of a lifetime, but you have no life," according to one of the two people. "She's sick of like — having drinks and then going back to work."

As far back as October Katie Miller had received calls from people inside the White House and Trump allies about the possibility that Wiles could leave. During those calls she suggested people should support Stephen Miller as a possible replacement, according to the person with direct knowledge.

While there had been speculation that Wiles might leave at the end of the year, the midterm wipeout made it all but certain.

One person close to the White House said replacing Wiles with Miller would show his political base that the president remains committed to the MAGA mission.

"It's a signal to the base that, you know, the White House hears you," said one of the two people close to the White House.

Megan Messerly contributed to this report.

articles.title: Democrats set sights on Elon Musk probe after midterm wins, but Pritzker draws a surprising line
articles.summary: Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., says he feels "pretty certain" at least one committee will investigate DOGE, calling Elon Musk's cost-cutting effort a catastrophe.
articles.body: Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., and Gov. JB Pritzker, D-Ill., are calling for an investigation into the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), previously led by Elon Musk, as talks have heated up among Democrats to launch a probe into the multibillionaire. "I had no specific plan," Raskin told Fox News Digital about the potential investigations. "Look…DOGE was a catastrophe for America, and at least one committee, I feel pretty certain, will investigate it. It needs to investigate it." Musk has emerged as a potential target of Democratic oversight, with some lawmakers calling for scrutiny of his time as head of the DOGE. The calls for an investigation come as Democrats have started rallying the party to look into corruption under the Trump administration after coming out victorious in midterms. SCHUMER, JEFFRIES SIDESTEP QUESTIONS ON NUKING FILIBUSTER, LAUNCHING ELON MUSK PROBE AFTER BLUE WAVE The tech CEO helped launch DOGE at the start of President Donald Trump's second term to root out waste and be more transparent about the federal government's spending. DOGE's efforts included deferred resignations and buyouts of employees at federal agencies and contributed to a significant downsizing of the federal workforce, which contracted by about 250,000 employees during 2025, according to the Government Accountability Office (GAO). Calls for investigations into DOGE also started over concerns about the department allegedly having access to Americans’ sensitive information. "I mean the whole thing was premised on a lie, and our private information was completely compromised by it," Raskin said. Despite Pritzker saying he had never "heard anything like that" about a potential probe of Musk and DOGE, he agreed that DOGE is worthy of an investigation. PROGRESSIVE GROUP'S 182-PAGE BLUEPRINT MAPS OUT POTENTIAL DEM INVESTIGATIONS INTO TRUMP, CORPORATE ALLIES "I think there should be a lot of inspection of what DOGE did," Pritzker told Fox News Digital. "I think that was pretty awful. " But Pritzker didn’t seem so sure that needing an investigation into DOGE also warranted an investigation into Musk himself. "I don't know about focusing on one person," Pritzker said when asked about investigating Musk. ELON MUSK BLAMES TRUMP, US MILITARY FOR SPACEX RESTRICTIONS UKRAINE WARNS COULD HAVE DEADLY CONSEQUENCES Democratic lawmakers have also suggested looking into Musk’s companies' multibillion-dollar contracts with the federal government and, more recently, his role in cutting internet access to the Ukrainian military. articles.title: 4 of nation's largest cities now led by socialist mayors after Tuesday's election, affecting tens of millions
articles.summary: Los Angeles and Washington, D.C., now join Seattle and New York City as top-20 U.S. cities led by DSA-affiliated socialist mayors in office.
articles.body: Two socialist mayors were elected in the United States on Tuesday in Los Angeles and Washington, D.C. which now means that four of the top 20 largest cities in the country have socialist leaders at the helm. Los Angeles Councilwoman Nithya Raman, a member of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) defeated incumbent mayor Karen Bass and will take office in December as mayor for the roughly 4 million residents of Los Angeles proper. Also victorious on Tuesday was DSA member Janeese Lewis George who coasted to victory to become mayor-elect of Washington, D.C., a city of roughly 700,000 residents. The list of socialist mayors in the top 20 most populous U.S. cities stands at 4, as George and Raman join Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani. DEMOCRATIC SOCIALIST SWEEPS INTO DC MAYOR'S OFFICE, SIGNALS OPENNESS TO WORKING WITH TRUMP In total, the four cities are home to roughly 14 million people. That figure does not include neighboring suburbs, which could still feel the effects of policies enacted within city limits through crime, real estate values and the broader business climate. Problems in a city can spill over into surrounding communities, while suburban residents who work in the city may also be directly affected. Counting the population in the metro areas of those four cities, roughly 44 million people could be affected either positively and negatively by the socialist policies enacted by the four mayors. DSA LEADER DISMISSES $49T COST ESTIMATE FOR SOCIALIST POLICIES AS A 'MADE-UP NUMBER' "This makes LA the fourth large city that will now have a socialist mayor, joining New York, Washington DC and Seattle," Heritage Foundation fellow Mike Gonzalez posted on X Thursday. "Chicago's mayor is a buffoon, but he doesn't identify as DSA. America used to be an impregnable fortress against Marxism, then Marxists took over universities." The socialist victories were not limited to city halls. Voters also elected seven DSA-backed or affiliated candidates to the House: Claire Valdez, Brand Lander and Darializa Avila Chevalier of New York, Chris Rabb of Pennsylvania, Melat Kiros of Colorado, Donavan McKinney of Michigan and Angela Gonzales-Torres of California. Several other candidates associated with socialist policies also entered Congress or were re-elected on Tuesday. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP A recent Fox News national poll indicated 32% of voters have a favorable view of socialism, with 64% seeing it in an unfavorable way. But the favorable rating matches an all-time high, first reached five years ago, since Fox News first began asking the question in 2019. And a September Gallup poll found that 43% of Americans had a positive image of socialism, the highest level since the polling organization began tracking the question in 2010. The Fox News poll found that 51% of voters had a favorable view of capitalism, compared with 32% who viewed socialism favorably. Another 46% had an unfavorable view of capitalism.

articles.title: GOP eyes Senate comeback after Democratic bloodbath, but another political nightmare could await
articles.summary: Democrats won at least 54 Senate seats Tuesday, but Republicans could flip the chamber in 2028 by sweeping six competitive states and holding the VP.
articles.body: Republican control of the Senate could return as soon as the 2028 general election, but only if the party can pull off a series of crucial victories in competitive races, a possibility that seems distant following Tuesday night's devastating Democratic sweep. As of publication, Democrats and independents who caucus with them have secured 54 Senate seats, a total that could grow to as many as 56 pending election calls in Mississippi and Alaska. Assuming Republicans hold the vice presidency in 2028, far from a guarantee, they would need to flip at least four seats during that election cycle to win the Senate back. While there are ample pick-up opportunities for Republicans in 2028 if the party can return to its typical national performance benchmarks, several vulnerable GOP-held seats could complicate their efforts to retake the upper chamber. DEMS FLIPS YET ANOTHER SENATE SEAT IN TRUMP COUNTRY AMID SWEEPING GOP UPSETS Iowa Sen. Chuck Grassley, for instance, turned 93 in September and faces a decision about whether to seek another term in 2028, when Republicans will be defending his seat in a state where Democrat Josh Turek just defeated Republican Ashley Hinson by roughly four percentage points. His departure before then could also give Iowa's incoming Democratic governor the opportunity to appoint a temporary replacement. Another possibility that could make the GOP's path back to a majority even more uncertain is the admission of Puerto Rico and Washington, D.C., to the union as full states. Such a move would likely require the Democratic-led Senate to abolish or overcome the legislative filibuster, something lawmakers representing more moderate or competitive states may balk at, as well as support in the House and either presidential approval or enough votes to override a veto. CHUCK SCHUMER AFTER SWEEPING DEMOCRATIC MIDTERM VICTORIES: 'I'LL BE RE-ELECTED AS MAJORITY LEADER' Even if the filibuster is done away with, President Donald Trump could veto admittance bills. Democrats currently lack the numbers to override such a veto. If Republicans lose the White House in 2028, however, Democrats could have a clearer path to advancing statehood for Puerto Rico and Washington, D.C., a move that would add four Senate seats and potentially complicate Republican efforts to win back the chamber, though significant political and legal obstacles would remain. Assuming none of that happens, Democrats will be defending six Senate seats that could offer Republicans potential pick-up opportunities in 2028. Republicans will have pick-up opportunities in New Hampshire, Nevada, Arizona, Georgia, Pennsylvania and Ohio that year. They will, however, be forced to defend vulnerable Senate seats in Wisconsin, Iowa and North Carolina. Indiana, which saw a significant blue shift, also has a Senate seat up for contention in 2028, while Nebraska, where independent Dan Osborn mounted a competitive but unsuccessful challenge to Republican Sen. Pete Ricketts on Tuesday, will not hold another regularly scheduled Senate election until 2030. While 2028 could deliver Republicans a majority if they play their cards right, another defeat on the scale of 2026 could put the Democratic Party dangerously close to the 60-vote threshold necessary to invoke cloture and counter a filibuster. "It may be unlikely, but I do think it's feasible," Heritage Action government relations director Chip Wyatt told Fox News Digital. "We're just as capable of having a night like the Democrats had on Tuesday in 2028. If anything, that election, the election we had on Tuesday has shown us that two years is a very, very long time in politics. think if you had told anybody in 2024 that this is what happened in 2028, they probably wouldn't believe you." For Republicans to have a good night in 2028, Wyatt argued that conservatives would have to focus on affordability issues while Democrats overstep their mandate by allowing the fringes of their party to dictate its policy agenda. Texas Sen. Ted Cruz took a similar line in reacting to Tuesday night's election results. "We will rebuild as a true blue-collar party, not by embracing socialism, but by being real free-market conservatives. The way we built the Texas economic miracle in the first place, and we will build and rebuild America as well," he said. "When the zealots overreach, and they will, we will stand ready to lead in the direction of freedom, of prosperity, of safety and security and common sense. We will return to a new dawn of freedom in America." 2030 features slightly fewer pick-ups for the GOP with a comparable number of states to defend. While Republicans will have pick-up opportunities in Arizona, Nevada, Wisconsin and Michigan, they will also be forced to defend seats in Texas, Ohio and Pennsylvania. MAJORITY LEADER THUNE SAYS SENATE GOP WON'T 'STAND IDLY BY' AS DEMOCRATS TAKE CONTROL OF CONGRESS The 2032 election will feature the same regularly scheduled Senate seats contested in 2026, giving Republicans another opportunity to retake deep-red states they blundered this year, such as Kansas and South Carolina. Historically, however, some moderate Democrats have managed to hang on to state-wide offices in typically red states, making a reversion far from a certainty. Former West Virginia Sen. Joe Manchin, for instance, managed to survive multiple GOP challenges in the deep-red state. Kansas and Kentucky, similarly, have Democratic governors that survived Republican challenges in races that received national attention. While many Republicans, and even some Democrats, have suggested liberal pick-ups in deep red states could be one-cycle wonders, Wyatt cautioned against complacency. "We should always assume the politicians want to get re-elected and so the senators in the deep red states that have been recently elected as Democrats are going to want to keep their seats and so they're going to be very strategic in how they vote and in what kind of bills they're introducing," Wyatt said. "In some of these deep red states, it's going to be difficult for [Democrats] to hold on to these seats ... Now granted, I've already said two years is a long time, six years is an even longer time. So who knows what kind of political landscape we're looking at in 2032 but Republicans should definitely start off with a strong advantage in many of these states ... But it's never wise to counter chickens before they hatch." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Electoral politics is famously unpredictable. Nobody in 2024, for instance, envisioned South Carolina or Kansas sending Democrats to the Senate in 2026. It is possible that the Republican path to a Senate majority, or lack thereof, will be comparably surprising.

articles.title: Did voters reject Christian nationalism? What the midterm results show
articles.summary: Some in the movement to boost Christianity's presence in public life were voted out of office, but advocates say there's much more work to be done.
articles.body:
Advocates for the separation of church and state have faced setbacks in recent years, but they say the results of the midterm elections have made them more optimistic about the road ahead.

It was a "huge repudiation of Trump, authoritarianism and Christian nationalism," said Annie Laurie Gaylor , co-founder and co-president of the Freedom From Religion Foundation .

The organization is one of many advocacy groups that have raised First Amendment concerns over efforts by President Donald Trump and his federal and state-level allies to boost their version of Christianity in the public square.

Several states have passed laws requiring Protestant versions of the Ten Commandments to be displayed in public school classrooms, for example, and members of Trump's Religious Liberty Commission frequently criticized what they described as a weaponization of the law against Christians under previous administrations.

The commission published a draft report in June that said religion has often been "treated not as a protected and valued contribution to public life, but as a problem or annoyance to be managed, restricted or sidelined."

Though it has its supporters – such as the Southern Baptist Convention's Ethics and Religious Liberty Commission , which said it "commends and supports many of the recommendations" in the report and that the commission "demonstrates a commitment to ensuring the retention and protection of the American value of religious liberty" – the commission has also faced heavy criticism from groups who say its work promotes Christian nationalism.

Interfaith Alliance, along with organizations including Muslims for Progressive Values and Hindus for Human Rights, sued the administration over the commission in February, arguing that it had an illegal lack of diversity by only having Christian and Jewish commissioners. A federal judge dismissed the lawsuit in July.

But now, Guthrie Graves-Fitzsimmons, Interfaith Alliance's vice president of programs and strategy, says it's a "beautiful day for religious freedom for all in America."

He and others who spoke to USA TODAY said the midterm elections could reshape the landscape for religious freedom, though they said the incoming Congress and state leaders have much work to do to reverse what they view as backslides for religious freedom in recent years.

Texas charting a 'new course for religious freedom'

They were especially heartened by results from Texas , where the "blue wave" – or "blue tsunami," as some pundits have called it – was particularly notable.

"In a state like Texas, where the Christian nationalism debate has been front and center and the fusion of far-right Christianity into public education has been so central, it's safe to say voters resoundingly rejected Christian nationalism in this election," said Rachel Laser , president and CEO of Americans United for Separation of Church and State .

Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, who signed the state's Ten Commandments legislation into law in June 2025, was voted out of office . He, along with Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis , also designated the Council on American-Islamic Relations, a Muslim civil rights group, as a foreign terrorist organization in late 2025.

A federal lawsuit in Texas accused the state of unconstitutional religious discrimination when the designation led to Islamic private schools initially being excluded from the state's school voucher program on the basis of a perceived affiliation with CAIR.

Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa, who will be the state's first Democratic governor in more than 30 years, opposed the Ten Commandments bill .

Texas Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick, who Trump named as chair of the Religious Liberty Commission, also lost his reelection bid .

Senator-elect James Talarico , a progressive Presbyterian who has called Christian nationalism a "betrayal of Jesus," defeated Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, who has rejected the notion that the Constitution requires a separation between church and state and sued to prevent CAIR from operating in Texas. Talarico proclaimed, "We defeated Goliath," in his victory speech.

"As Texas charts a new course for religious freedom, it will be a shining light for the whole nation," Graves-Fitzsimmons said.

Who is James Talarico? Meet the new Texas Senator

Concerns are 'not going to evaporate' despite midterm wins

Now that the midterms are over, advocates said the focus must shift to reversing the efforts of the past few years and preserving religious freedom for the long haul.

"We are going to have to do a lot of work to keep this going in two years," Gaylor said.

Steven Emmert , executive director of the lobbying group Secular Coalition For America , said his organization intends to work with the new lawmakers, as well as existing ones, to promote a separation between church and state. He would like to see more lawmakers join the Congressional Freethought Caucus , which currently has around three dozen members and has a shared mission.

He also hoped the election would prompt lawmakers to recognize the growing influence of religious "nones."

"Part of the work of SCA is to make sure they become aware of that, because clearly it's going to matter in future elections as well," he said.

Freedom Forum does not provide editorial input. Reach BrieAnna at bjfrank@usatoday.com and @brieannafrank on X and Bluesky.

articles.title: See Trump's state-by-state approval days after GOP's midterm drubbing
articles.summary: Trump’s unpopularity continues climb following his political party's trouncing in Tuesday's midterms. See which states still approve of the president.
articles.body:
Only days after Democrats handed the GOP one of its largest electoral defeats in decades, President Donald Trump's unpopularity has continued to grow, with his net approval rating sitting positive in only eight states.

According to the latest Civiqs state-by-state tracker , Trump has a negative net approval rating in 39 states. Three states are evenly split with a net approval rating of zero, while the president has positive net approval in just eight states.

Trump remains positive in Arkansas, Idaho, Kansas, North Dakota, Oklahoma, Utah, West Virginia and Wyoming, all states he carried in the past three presidential elections.

Of the states backing the president, Wyoming remains his strongest state, with his net approval rating at 17%; meanwhile, Oklahoma and Kansas are among his weakest, with Trump sitting at a net approval rating of just 1%.

Here's Trump's approval by state following a lopsided midterms.

Trump's unpopularity continues to grow in several states he carried in the 2024 presidential election, with Nov. 3's electoral drubbing only the latest example of his continued fall in the polls.

The president has had better weeks, as his polling numbers and political party have taken a hit.

Rather than seeing a slew of bad approval polls like in other recent weeks, Trump instead got an electoral bashing, with his Republican Party seeing one of its worst nights in recent history.

As of Friday, Nov. 6, Democrats are within striking distance of 56 Senate seats , with tight races in Alaska and historically deep-red Mississippi still too close to call. In the House of Representatives, Democrats are on track to win their largest majority since 2008, at 249 seats with more than 20 races still to be called.

Among the highest-profile seats Democrats gained on Tuesday were historically Republican Senate seats in Texas, South Carolina, Iowa and Kansas, where Democrats had not won a Senate seat since the 1930s.

Fernando Cervantes Jr. is a trending news reporter for USA TODAY. Reach him at fernando.cervantes@usatodayco.com and follow him on X @fern_cerv_.

articles.title: TREY GOWDY: The midterms were a painful lesson that Republicans can't skip learning
articles.summary: How do you go from winning the Electoral College and the popular vote in 2024 and being trusted with the gift to govern to historic losses in a relatively short period of time?
articles.body: PROGRAMMING ALERT: Watch Trey Gowdy discuss this topic and more on "Sunday Night in America with Trey Gowdy" on Nov. 8 at 9 pm ET. Losing is the toughest teacher; so tough, you only want to take the class once. For Republicans, Tuesday night was excruciating. Yes, history said, "Be prepared for losses." Yes, the mood of the voters was anger and uncertainty. But I did not talk to anyone who was prepared for what happened, either in terms of the sheer loss or the margin of the loss. Senate candidates in red states lost by unheard-of numbers. Long-serving and hard-working Republican House members like Virginia Foxx, Mike Turner and Richard Hudson were caught up in the tidal wave. South Carolina, North Carolina, Texas, Kansas and Ohio are red states in most presidential cycles. Not last Tuesday night. It was as thorough a whipping as I can recall in my lifetime. So why? What are the lessons to be learned, and what are the cautions for the Democrats? As it turns out, there are parallels between the two. CONSERVATIVES STUNNED BY 'CATASTROPHIC' MIDTERM BLUE TSUNAMI, BLAME TRUMP'S IRAN WAR, HIGH GAS PRICES How do you go from winning the Electoral College and the popular vote in a presidential race and being trusted with the gift to govern to historic losses in a relatively short period of time? President Trump did so and easily could claim a "mandate" on certain issues when he was victorious in November 2024. People want a secure border. People want violent offenders deported without delay. People want a rational immigration policy that rewards the right people and is rooted in fundamental humanity. By humanity, I mean showing dignity to those women and men who have been cutting the lawns, cleaning the hotel rooms and working in service industries while also abiding by our criminal laws. By humanity, I mean protecting American citizens from violent criminals – legally here or otherwise. President Trump’s first DHS secretary wrote last Tuesday night, "We lost because we were ‘too successful.’" It is that type of thinking that turns a one-cycle loss into decades of minority status. When people voted for border security, they were not including glitzy, self-serving ad campaigns focused on boosting personal political ambitions. When people chose Donald Trump in 2024, they gave not one thought to the possibility that Americans would be shot in cars or on the street and labeled domestic terrorists before even an initial investigation was conducted. It is absurd to assert Republicans lost in South Carolina, Texas, Kansas, Ohio, North Carolina and Michigan because "we were too successful." Losing can teach you. But only if you bother to show up for class. Every win is not a mandate. Every mandate is not a license to do whatever you want, regardless of the issue. President Trump was elected in 2024 because he promised to make life more affordable and safer for hard-working Americans who need not worry about the California billionaire tax. They are simply trying to raise families and meet their societal and familial obligations. There was not even a whiff in the 2024 exit polls about voters clamoring for those in government to engage in more self-enrichment, pursue naked personal political ambition, or use public office for anything other than true public service. FOX NEWS VOTER POLL: 2026 MIDTERM ELECTIONS USHER IN A BLUE WAVE AS DEMOCRATS WIN CONTROL OF CONGRESS The forensic pathologists were up early Wednesday morning performing their autopsies. Some blamed the war in Iran for being deeply unpopular. Good. War should be unpopular and rarely waged. But being unpopular and being incorrect are two different things. There was no war with Iran. There were nights of strikes, a heroic pilot rescue, and blockades of the Strait of Hormuz. American service members lost their lives as a direct consequence of Iranian action, but that has been the case for decades. Iran has been killing Americans and giving aid and comfort to those who do so for nearly 50 years. That is precisely why the president insisted, "No more" and "No nuclear Iran." People can take whatever position they like on those issues, and reasonable minds can differ even within the same political party. But let us not forget that Iran has been a global pariah for nearly half a century, and I have yet to meet the person (outside of a few terrorist groups) who thinks it is a good idea for theocratic despots to have nuclear weapons. LIZ PEEK: THERE MAY BE A SILVER LINING IN TRUMP'S BRUTAL MIDTERM DEFEAT What is just as plausible is that voters got vertigo from all the fits and starts. War was on and then off. There was peace but then missiles. There was an MOU that took longer to draft than it lasted in effect. Was it possible Americans needed to be convinced that all other means of reining Iran in had been explored and exhausted? CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION What is just as plausible is that the American people coveted a deeper explanation of why engagement with Iran was necessary now. Perhaps Iran was a drag on the election, but not nearly as much as perceived corruption, higher gas prices, and a sense that no one was listening. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP And that leads to the cautionary tale for Democrats. Winning does not equal a mandate. Sometimes it simply means voters hated you slightly less than the other team. With the right candidates, South Carolina, North Carolina, Texas, Kansas, Ohio, and Georgia can easily be red again. Failing to heed the lessons of why you lost, casting blame in all the wrong places, and not engaging in serious self-reflection will most likely prolong that color change. articles.title: Democratic senator-elect calls Trump 'unserious fool' while defending combative political style
articles.summary: Abdul El-Sayed told Pod Save America that Democrats must treat Trump as an "unserious fool" and stop clinging to outdated political decorum.
articles.body: Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic senator-elect from Michigan, leaned into accusations of acting cocky on the path to victory over Republican candidate Mike Rogers, citing a need to push back on President Donald Trump’s manner of communication during an appearance on Pod Save America. "Long ago, you predicted that you would win this race by seven points, which at the time seemed like a pretty cocky and ill-considered thing to say. Then you won the race by seven points. People are still calling you cocky," podcast host Jon Favreau said during his interview with El-Sayed. "How do you see yourself?" "I think there is a responsibility that we have to engage with [Trump] as the unserious fool that he is," El-Sayed replied. EL-SAYED MOCKS TRUMP, VANCE AND ROGERS IN GLOATING VICTORY SPEECH SIGNALING COMBATIVE TONE IN SENATE El-Sayed’s response sheds light on his view of his own campaign and the tone that he believes Democrats need to adopt to counter Trump’s presence in American politics. It also raises questions of whether El-Sayed’s campaign strategies will yield results in Congress. In his view, Trump has changed the style of acceptable communication. In turn, he accused Democrats of being hesitant to abandon a kind of decorum to fight fire with fire. "I just think there’s a responsibility for us to walk out of 'The West Wing' episode that our politics used to feel like and into the reality of where we are," El-Sayed said, referring to a a television drama known for its idealistic portrayal of American politics. "I say that because if you’ve ever watched a bully in a room, if you don’t stand up to the bully, it’s not like the bully will just go away. The bully just gets stronger," El-Sayed said. During his campaign, El-Sayed repeatedly pointed a finger at Trump for, in his view, ushering in a new age of political rhetoric. But that view also preceded his Senate bid. TRUMP DOMINATES EL-SAYED'S ATTACKS AGAINST ROGERS, BUT GOP RIVAL OFFERS UNEXPECTED POLICY SPLIT He once accused President Donald Trump of inciting terrorism in a 2020 interview, citing a foiled plot to kidnap Gov. Gretchen Whitmer. "These are terrorists; we have to call them that. We have to recognize that that is what the face of terrorism looks like right now. We have to step up against it," El-Sayed said. "We gotta ask: why are these people getting radicalized? Well, there must be some radical, extremist cleric out there who may be tweeting up a storm about all the things that they think need to be done, like liberating Michigan." Although President Donald Trump did not call for any kind of violence against Whitmer, El-Sayed said he believed the president was at least partially responsible, pointing to a tweet Trump had made six months before the discovered plot. "LIBERATE MICHIGAN!" Trump wrote in a post on Twitter, the social media platform now known as X. The post was one of a series calling to "liberate" Virginia and Minnesota from COVID-19 restrictions imposed by Democratic governors. According to FBI comments to local media, the plot originated before Trump's post. Even so, El-Sayed called the posts emblematic of a cultural toxicity that had made violence more likely. "The idea that people would threaten her safety because she was willing to stand up to keep us all healthy is, to me, the example of what the kind of toxicity that we see out of Donald Trump creates," El-Sayed said. MAJORITY LEADER THUNE SAYS SENATE GOP WON'T 'STAND IDLY BY' AS DEMOCRATS TAKE CONTROL OF CONGRESS A spokesperson for El-Sayed did not immediately respond to requests for comment on whether he believed in a red line for what kind of rhetoric Democrats should refrain from using. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Having won his U.S. Senate election, El-Sayed will be sworn into office on Jan. 3, 2027, the start of the 120th Congress.

articles.summary: From the East Coast to the Midwest to the West, unions are celebrating.
articles.body:
Lost amid the headlines and endless midterm election punditry is the reality that Tuesday was a big night for labor unions across the board. With both major parties increasingly seeking to embrace organized labor, the 2026 elections foreshadow a potential watershed moment in our modern labor politics.

The pro-union momentum started on the East Coast with two proposed state constitutional amendments on the ballot in Vermont and Maryland. In Vermont, voters approved —by a nearly 3-to-1 margin —Proposal 3, which creates a state constitutional right to collectively bargain, while simultaneously prohibiting any future laws that might get in the way of this right. The constitutional amendment also bars the state Legislature from enacting a right-to-work law going forward.

In Maryland, voters passed—again, by almost a 3-to-1 margin —their own constitutional amendment that requires the governor's proposed budget to fully fund any collective bargaining agreements for state employees (it's unclear if the state legislature would then be required to follow suit and fund those agreements in full). If government employees and the state are unable to reach an agreement during the collective bargaining process, the amendment empowers an arbitrator to dictate terms to each side through a process that's known as binding interest arbitration.

Under current Maryland law, the governor is required to deliver a balanced budget proposal to the state Legislature. The new amendment could now create scenarios where collective bargaining agreements or binding interest arbitration locks in high wages and fringe benefits—all while tying the governor's and legislature's hands when it comes to making important fiscal decisions in the state budget. This could theoretically lead to the governor and Legislature having to impose drastic cuts in other important government services to make ends meet.

In the Midwest, Wisconsin voters ushered a Democratic trifecta into office, giving the party complete control of the legislative and executive branches. Democratic Gov.-elect David Crowley explicitly campaigned on overturning former Gov. Scott Walker's famous 2011 collective bargaining reforms. Although Democrats have not controlled the state Legislature in Madison since 2010, they now do, which should give Crowley the needed votes to follow through. (Even if Walker's reforms are not legislatively repealed, they may soon be invalidated by the state's left-leaning Supreme Court).

Out West, Colorado elected Democrat Phil Weiser as its new governor, which could presage the state's own sea change in labor law. Colorado has long operated under a hybrid right-to-work law called the Labor Peace Act. Traditional right-to-work laws prohibit so-called union security clauses in collective bargaining agreements, which require employees to pay union dues as a condition of employment.

Under Colorado's system , a union can be certified with a bare majority of support from workers, but the inclusion of union security clauses in a bargaining agreement requires supermajority support among workers. Colorado's Democratic Legislature has twice sent bills to the governor to repeal the Labor Peace Act's second-vote requirement, only to be vetoed each time by moderate Democrat Gov. Jared Polis. Unlike Polis, Weiser supports the second-vote repeal , so state lawmakers can simply wait out the end of Polis' term.

Finally, Nevada saw its own Democratic trifecta elected to office. Democratic Gov.-elect Aaron Ford has gone on record with his desire to repeal the state's right-to-work law. With unanimous Democratic control of the state government, it appears that Nevada's right-to-work law is likewise on borrowed time.

Perhaps most ominous are the developments at the federal level. Prior to the election, a bill called the Faster Labor Contracts Act (FLCA) started to pick up steam in Congress. The legislation is sponsored by pro-union Sen. Josh Hawley (R–Mo.) and has a handful of Republican supporters on Capitol Hill. The FLCA cleared the House of Representatives but so far has stalled out in the Senate due to lack of votes.

But now, depending on how the remaining uncalled Senate races shake out, the FLCA may be within a stone's throw of President Donald Trump's desk. If Democrats secure 56 seats in the Senate, that puts theoretical support for the FLCA at 58 votes once Republican support is factored in (in addition to Hawley, Sen. Bernie Moreno (R–Ohio) is also a co-sponsor of the FLCA).

This means that only two more GOP votes would be needed to clear the Senate's 60-vote cloture threshold and send the bill to the White House. Given the GOP's ongoing courtship of organized labor—both in Congress and in the White House—the FLCA now has a plausible road to passage.

The FLCA would establish a binding interest arbitration system like that enacted by voters in Maryland, only this version would apply to the private sector workforce—an unprecedented first in American labor law. America's legal tradition has long conceptualized labor contracts as voluntary agreements entered into by employers and employees. If the FLCA passes, a government-backed arbitration panel could force binding terms on parties—a longtime desire of labor unions.

It may seem easy to chalk off organized labor's big night on Tuesday as a natural byproduct of a Democratic wave. But as the FLCA shows, the political math is no longer that simple. In fact, the FLCA could be one of the most consequential bipartisan laws to come out of Washington post-2026.

That, combined with all the state-level developments, shows how big Tuesday night could be in the history of modern labor politics.

articles.title: MIKE DAVIS: Lame-duck Senate has unfinished business and a ticking clock
articles.summary: Chuck Schumer will likely block every Trump judicial nominee once Democrats take the Senate, making the next two months critical for the GOP.
articles.body: On Jan. 3, 2027, leftist Democrats will take control of the U.S. Senate. The stakes could not be higher. Outgoing Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., must use every remaining day to confirm all of President Trump's pending judicial nominees. That means 23 judges, four for the circuit courts and 19 for the district courts, before the gavel changes hands. Make no mistake about what comes next. Incoming Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., will block any confirmation to the courts of appeals. He likely won't spare the district courts either. Senate Republicans either finish the judicial job now, or they leave these seats open for the left if Democrats win back the White House in 2028. Appellate courts are the most consequential. They get the final word in the vast majority of cases. The Supreme Court grants only about 1% of all petitions for review. For nearly every litigant in federal court in America, the circuit court is the last stop. TRUMP AIMS TO ELEVATE FEDERAL JUDGE LEE RUDOFSKY TO COURT OF APPEALS FOR THE EIGHTH CIRCUIT President Trump has nominated four outstanding jurists to strengthen key appellate benches: Anna St. John and Todd Butler to the Fifth Circuit, Lee Rudofsky to the Eighth Circuit, and Dan Domenico to the Tenth Circuit. St. John, Rudofsky, and Domenico already serve with distinction on the district courts in Louisiana, Arkansas, and Colorado. All four are well prepared to step into these roles. They will succeed judges who have given the country decades of distinguished service: Fifth Circuit Judges Leslie Southwick and Kurt Engelhardt, Eighth Circuit Judge Bobby Shepherd, and Tenth Circuit Judge Timothy Tymkovich. Their long and exemplary tenures merit our deep gratitude. UNDER-THE-RADAR IMPLICATION OF DEM BLUE WAVE MEANS 'ZERO' CHANCE GOP ACCOMPLISHES CRITICAL GOAL, EXPERTS WARN Outgoing Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Chuck Grassley, R-Iowa, is the king of oversight and the undisputed heavyweight champion of shepherding nominees through the confirmation gauntlet. He has already scheduled two November hearings to handle an expanded slate, and he is taking heat from Democrats for doing it. Grassley has done his part. Now his colleagues must do theirs. Sen. John Boozman and his fellow Arkansas Republican Sen. Tom Cotton have raised questions about Rudofsky, and every senator has the right to do his due diligence. But the calendar leaves no more room for deliberation. Rudofsky is a constitutionalist stalwart, and he has earned swift approval. If this nomination stalls, a left-wing judicial activist could eventually take this crucially important federal appellate seat. Sen. Boozman and his colleagues should move Rudofsky without further delay. HUGH HEWITT: THE MIDTERMS ARE ONE MONTH OUT — YOU NEED TO KNOW THE STAKES District courts matter too. The slate is set, and the work that remains is simple. Republican senators must show up for every committee vote, advance this slate out of the Judiciary Committee and confirm every one of these nominees on the Senate floor. The pieces are in place. Get it done, quickly. Democrats wrote this playbook. In the 2024 lame-duck session, after Republicans had won a Senate majority starting in January 2025, then-Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Richard Durbin, D-Illinois, ruthlessly rammed through several judges. The votes kept coming until just a few days before Christmas, and Schumer enthusiastically led the way. The left has no standing to complain today when the GOP rightly returns the favor. Given the chance, Schumer would do it all again. Everyone knows it. Many Republican incumbents leave office in January after years of service to their states. Crucial work remains. These judges will sit for decades and dramatically shape the law. Senators have a solemn responsibility to confirm these exceptional nominees. A leftist president must not get to stack these seats with radicals. Constitutionalists must hold these lifetime appointments. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The next two years will be bleak for judicial nominees, and bleak in plenty of other ways. The next two months must be bright. Confirming these outstanding judges will be the lasting legacy of these outgoing senators. CLICK FOR MORE FROM MIKE DAVIS

articles.title: House GOP erupts at Stephen Miller as Trump elevates him after midterm massacre: 'Megalomaniac'
articles.summary: House Republicans expressed shock and anger after Trump promoted Stephen Miller to chief of staff following the GOP's historic midterm losses.
articles.body: Several Republican lawmakers are fuming over President Donald Trump’s elevation of Stephen Miller to be his chief of staff. "Horrible decision," Rep. Marlin Stutzman, R-Ind., told Fox News Digital on Friday after Trump announced his decision. A Republican lawmaker who was granted anonymity to speak candidly said they were in "utter disbelief." Tensions were rising against Miller in the wake of Republicans’ terrible performance in Tuesday’s midterm elections. Multiple House Republicans who spoke with Fox News Digital just moments before his promotion said Miller, who spearheads Trump’s immigration policy, should be fired. TRUMP NAMES STEPHEN MILLER NEW WHITE HOUSE CHIEF OF STAFF, REPLACING SUSIE WILES When later asked about his promotion, one House Republican who said Miller should be fired replied simply with a facepalm emoji. Republicans suffered historic losses that saw both the House and Senate fall into Democrats’ hands in the new Congress. Democrats are on pace to win more than 250 seats in the House and at least 54 in the Senate. AMERICA SAW THE BLUE WAVE COMING — BUT DRASTICALLY UNDERESTIMATED THE EXTENT OF THE DEM TSUNAMI And while voter analyses have shown that Trump’s war in Iran and tariffs played the biggest roles in turning people away from the GOP, his handling of illegal immigration served to alienate voters in key areas. That’s in no small part due to Hispanic and Latino voters turning their backs on Republicans in places like Texas that shifted massively toward Democrats in this election cycle. "Because of his immigration positions, I just think we ruined a lot of our goodwill with Latino voters," Stutzman said. The second GOP lawmaker told Fox News Digital that Miller ignored multiple warnings from House Republicans in the past, arguing that Trump’s immigration crackdown is what voters asked for. "I've been in several group meetings where a lot of us have told him, ‘Your immigration enforcement policies are backfiring back home, our people are mad, our businesses are mad — even in deep red districts — and it is impacting not just the voters, but the donors, and everybody top to bottom," that GOP lawmaker said. "But it looked to me like Stephen Miller was only after numbers … he would not listen to us." Other Republicans who spoke with Fox News Digital also criticized Miller but did not go as far as to say he should be fired. REPUBLICANS TURN ON TRUMP AFTER DEVASTATING MIDTERM LOSSES HAND DEMOCRATS CONTROL OF CONGRESS "I think he's greatly hurt the administration and cost us many seats on Tuesday," retiring Rep. Don Bacon, R-Neb., told Fox News Digital before news of Miller’s promotion broke. "He took an immigration policy that favored the president 2:1 in the public, over-reached and made it 2:1 unfavorable." "Many Republicans don’t like him," Bacon added when asked about his promotion. Miller is widely known as Trump’s right hand on immigration policy, including earlier this year when the administration faced bipartisan backlash over its handling of anti-immigration enforcement protests in places like Minneapolis. Several Republicans, particularly those running in battleground districts, had called for Trump to limit deportations to illegal immigrants who have committed crimes while in the United States. A fourth GOP lawmaker said, "Stephen is a megalomaniac who should have never been given the keys to the Ferrari. That being said, he's not the reason why we lost...no one knows who Stephen Miller is in our districts." Various other administration officials also got their share of blame in the fallout from Tuesday’s midterm massacre, including Secretary of War Pete Hegseth and Trump himself. But the president and people in his orbit have blamed candidate quality, arguing that in many cases the president campaigned harder than some of the people he supported did for themselves. And in his Truth Social post announcing Miller’s promotion, Trump called him one of his "most trusted advisors." He later told reporters Miller would "do a great job." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP When Fox News Digital reached the White House for comment, spokeswoman Lauren Bis said Miller "has been a key player in delivering on President Trump’s America First agenda since day one." "He has spearheaded the administration’s crime crackdown including in D.C. and Memphis, record setting deregulation, unleashed American energy, dismantled drug cartels, and secured our border. In his new role, he will continue to deliver historic successes for the American people," Bis said. Bis also pointed to a list of positive comments about Miller by administration officials and members of Congress. "Very grateful to Susie for her friendship and service to the president and our country. Stephen Miller is an amazing patriot and will do great things. Congrats to him on a well deserved promotion!" Vice President JD Vance said. "Stephen Miller has built a proven record focused on securing our border, combating crime, and advancing a now much-needed common-sense conservative agenda for our country," House Freedom Caucus Chairman Andy Harris said. A White House official told Fox News Digital Miller had experience working with Democrats on the D.C. Safe and Beautiful Task Force and that he has been a "valuable, trusted aide" since 2016.

articles.title: California prosecutors slam Newsom's death row commutations, accuse governor of putting 'politics over people'
articles.summary: District attorneys and law enforcement unions blast Gov. Gavin Newsom's mass commutation of 548 death row sentences as a betrayal of victims' families.
articles.body: District attorneys and law enforcement unions across California have publicly condemned Gov. Gavin Newsom following his announcement to commute the sentences of 548 death row inmates, a decision one prosecutor called a slap in the face to victims' families. Newsom’s sweeping order to commute the condemned inmates to life in prison without the possibility of parole has drawn intense criticism alongside praise from anti-death penalty advocates. "I think it's all about politics, sadly. Politics is over people in this case, and that's a real sad state of affairs," San Luis Obispo County District Attorney Dan Dow told Fox News Digital. ALABAMA GOVERNOR COMMUTES DEATH SENTENCE AS DOUBTS EMERGE ABOUT EVIDENCE IN MURDER CONVICTION In an open letter detailing his decision, Newsom said California's capital punishment system is fundamentally at odds with the state's principles. "After nearly 30 years in public office, I have come to understand the limits of what government can justly accomplish," Newsom wrote. "I take this action because I firmly believe that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California’s values, undermines the foundations of our legal system, and diminishes each of us." POPE LEO DENOUNCES DEATH PENALTY AS 'INADMISSIBLE' AHEAD OF PENTAGON'S PLANNED LIVESTREAMED EXECUTION Upon taking office in 2019, Newsom issued an executive moratorium on capital punishment. California has not carried out an execution since 2006. The backlash to the governor's announcement was immediate. FLORIDA PUTS 77-YEAR-OLD MAN TO DEATH FOR DEPUTY'S MURDER AS STATE CLOSES IN ON EXECUTION RECORD "Justice will not have been served for these victims, dozens of them in San Diego County," said Lt. Jared Wilson, president of the San Diego Police Officers Association. "Their last memories were of these evil, evil men who took their lives. What Gavin Newsom has done is awful." Wilson and other law enforcement officials strongly criticized the blanket clemency, citing cases like that of Jesse Michael Gomez, who was sentenced to death for the 2016 murder of San Diego police officer Jonathan "J.D." De Guzman. "Californians have been asked on two separate ballot initiatives to abolish the death penalty, and both times they have chosen to keep it for the most serious crimes," said Los Angeles County District Attorney Nathan Hochman. "Until the law is changed, my office will continue to evaluate every death penalty-eligible case with the rigor, care, and restraint these decisions demand." NEW YORK BILLS COULD ABOLISH LIFE WITHOUT PAROLE FOR SERIAL KILLERS AND COP KILLERS, CRITICS WARN Orange County District Attorney Todd Spitzer called the commutations "mercy for the wolves … while inflicting the ultimate act of cruelty on the sheep," saying voters in California have upheld the death penalty in recent years. Riverside County Sheriff Chad Bianco, who previously ran for governor, noted that 127 inmates on California’s death row were sentenced for crimes committed in his county. "These sentences were not handed down without due process," he said. "They followed extensive investigations, lengthy trials, evidence presented in court, and decisions made by juries and judges. "Yet, with one sweeping executive decision, the governor has chosen to override those outcomes, disregarding the voices of victims’ families, the work of prosecutors, and the pursuit of justice that took years to achieve." Among the 548 inmates whose sentences were commuted are two men convicted in San Luis Obispo County: Michael Whisenhunt, 61, who was sentenced to death for the 1995 torture and murder of his girlfriend's 1-year-old daughter, Kesha Gurke; and Rex Krebs, 60, who was convicted in the brutal slayings of two female college students. CHARLES MANSON CULT FOLLOWER BRUCE DAVIS, CONVICTED IN TWO 1969 KILLINGS, DIES BEHIND BARS AT 83 Dow noted that families of the victims were neither consulted nor notified prior to Newsom's public announcement. "I was just sickened, frankly, for the crime victims in California who were slapped in the face by our governor," Dow said. JUDGE BLOCKS ALABAMA'S NITROGEN GAS EXECUTION METHOD, RULES IT IS UNCONSTITUTIONALLY CRUEL Addressing arguments from anti-death penalty groups who contend that capital punishment is inherently flawed and racially biased, Dow defended the current legal framework.
