articles.title: Ukraine's power network suffers further damage after fresh Russian strikes
articles.summary: The attacks come before Ukrainian and Russian delegations are due to take part in trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi next week.
articles.body:
Overnight drone and ballistic missile attacks damaged Ukrainian energy infrastructure, President Volodymyr Zelenskyhas said, causing blackouts and disrupting water supplies.

Zelensky said 12 Ukrainian regions came under attack with the capital Kyiv hit hardest.

Nine people are reported to have been hurt across the country, including one child, in the wave of attacks that consisted of more than 30 ballistic missiles and over 170 drones.

The attacks come before Ukrainian and Russian delegations are due to take part in trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi next week.

Zelensky wrote on Telegram that Moscow was preparing for the talks by launching attacks on Ukraine's "critical infrastructure".

Temperatures are dropping in Ukraine, and parts of the country have had the first winter snow.

"The situation in the capital is difficult, with disruptions to electricity, water, and heating supplies. Residential buildings, the North Bridge, and a kindergarten have been damaged," Zelensky said.

"In the Kyiv region, there were strikes on substations that connect the Rivne and Khmelnytsky nuclear power plants to Kyiv and central Ukraine."

In his latest update, Kyiv's Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the city's water supply system is back to operating normally. He also said around 60% of the city's apartment buildings were connected to the heating system.

The energy minister, Denys Shmyhal, said there were power cuts in five regions but did not say how many homes were affected.

Zelensky added that beyond Kyiv, substations were damaged in Vinnytsia, Zhytomyr, Rivne, Kharkiv and Dnipro regions.

The latest attacks come after US First Lady Melania Trump hosted Russian and Ukrainian delegations at the White House on Thursday.

She called for a "more enduring" ceasefire in Ukraine following a truce last week in the southern region of Kherson.

She thanked both Zelensky and Russian President Vladimir Putin, making no reference to the origins of the war, which began when Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, which has caused thousands of civilian casualties and the displacement of millions.

Hundreds of residents of the Russian-occupied Ukrainian town of Oleshky facing starvation and constant bombardment were able to evacuate during a six-day ceasefire , which both Moscow and Kyiv credited Trump with brokering.

"The lives of innocent people must transcend the division of war. I hope Oleshky inspires greater peace," she said.

Earlier this week, a number of people were killed when glide bombs hit an aid centre near Zaporizhzhia , with the death toll rising to 55 as teams search deeper into the ruins.

Zelensky added in his Telegram post on Saturday following the latest attacks that Ukraine was counting on increased bilateral support from the United States.

He wrote: "We are counting on unity between both parties on issues of security, support for Ukraine, condemnation of Russian aggression, and increased sanctions pressure on Putin.

"The resolve and consistency of the United States in supporting Ukraine are of great importance in bringing peace closer."

Meanwhile, Zelenksy's spokesperson would not be drawn on reports that the Ukrainian president is to be invited to the UK for a state visit next year.

articles.title: Trump’s elevation of Stephen Miller is a middle finger to millions of voters
articles.summary: Architect of Trump’s far-right immigration agenda is now most powerful unelected figure in government – it suggests White House is moving to a war footing
articles.body:
Donald Trump just gave the middle finger to millions of American voters.

Any other president who suffered the kind of drubbing at the polls that Trump did this week might have felt at least a sliver of humility – and perhaps even an obligation to work with the new opposition in Congress.

But not for the first time in his political career, Trump veered in the opposite direction. On Friday he made Stephen Miller, condemned by Democrats and civil rights groups as a white nationalist, one of the most powerful unelected officials in Washington by naming him White House chief of staff .

Miller is the architect of Trump's far-right, nativist immigration agenda. He is, therefore, arguably the architect of the blue wave that engulfed Republicans in Tuesday's midterm elections as voters – including many Latinos – expressed their disgust. Yet instead of firing Miller, Trump promoted him.

It was a declaration of war. Miller, 41, is a longtime proponent of the presidential authority that Trump has spent the past two years expanding at the expense of Congress. In 2017 he declared : "The powers of the president to protect our country are very substantial and will not be questioned."

Now Republicans' catastrophic defeat is likely to leave Trump more reliant on unilateral executive action than ever to advance his domestic agenda.

"In a lot of ways Stephen Miller has been the id to Trump's authoritarian impulses and machinations," Kurt Bardella , an adviser to Democrats in Texas, said. "I have to imagine that anointing this person chief of staff – the most powerful non-elected position in all of government – is a signal that they intend to double down on that authoritarianism.

"You're going to see a lot of executive orders, unilateral action and stress testing of the checks and balances system continue for the final two years of his presidency."

Trump's second term has presented a concerted effort to dismantle those checks and balances that have traditionally constrained the occupant of the White House. He has signed 292 executive orders in less than two years, more than in his entire first term and a record pace for a modern presidency.

He has bypassed Congress on military action and tariffs, withheld congressionally approved spending, deployed the National Guard against the will of state authorities, politicised the justice department, punished critics and challenged judicial independence. Congress, dominated by Republicans reluctant to confront him, offered little resistance.

But this week's landslide , the biggest in a midterm election since Watergate, puts Democrats back in charge of the House of Representatives and Senate. That the elections were free and fair, and that Trump did not dispute the result, was itself a victory for democracy.

Democrats will now seek to rein in the president and block his legislative agenda, bringing them into direct conflict with Miller, who was already a hugely powerful deputy chief of staff at the White House and now takes over from Susie Wiles .

Miller has been a champion of the Iran war and prominent voice on many of the president's other priorities, including countering diversity initiatives and targeting transgender rights. He is reportedly one of a small group of White House staffers who approve all executive orders.

He is best known for driving the ‌immigration crackdown in Trump's second term, setting ‌a target of 3,000 arrests per day – far above levels under previous administrations. He has pushed Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) to target anybody in ‌the country illegally, not just those with criminal records.

There are limits on what Democrats can do to stop the immigration drive since the One Big Beautiful Bill Act included major increases for Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) that will keep it funded for the rest of Trump's term.

Even so, they will now chair House committees with the ability to launch investigations, issue subpoenas and hold high profile hearings. Along with ICE, they might scrutinise Jeffrey Epstein files and the department of government efficiency (Doge). They have also vowed to look at how Trump and his family have become wealthier since he returned to office.

The appointment of the pugnacious Miller as Trump's consigliere suggests that the White House is moving to a war footing. He is likely to marshal a team of lawyers and attack Democrats by accusing them of weaponising the deep state against the president. As a frequent guest on the conservative Fox News network, he will also wage war in the court of public opinion.

"Trump's decision to elevate Stephen Miller means that he's spoiling for a fight with Democrats and they're going to just rely on executive action to try and push their agenda through," said David Cohen, a political science professor at the University of Akron in Ohio , who studies the American presidency and White House staffing.

Cohen added: "It's a White House that doesn't seek out cooperation with Congress. It's their way or the highway, essentially, and it's possible Stephen Miller is relishing this because he's a believer in the unitary presidency and executive presidential action and he views this as a way where he can expand the powers of the presidency."

Trump is not the first president to seek to consolidate authority. Arthur Schlesinger Jr's 1973 book The Imperial Presidency warned that an accumulation of presidential power threatened the constitutional separation of powers.

In 1989 the American Enterprise Institute thinktank published The Fettered Presidency , a counterpoint arguing that legal and congressional constraints had unduly weakened the executive. It helped inspire a modern conservative drive to expand presidential authority, which accelerated under George W Bush and was subsequently exploited by Barack Obama as congressional gridlock made legislating increasingly difficult.

The combination of Trump and Miller, however, takes the concept of an American Caesar to a new extreme – and flies in the face of the verdict delivered by the electorate on Tuesday.

"It's a step that I find hard to fathom except as the president giving the middle finger to the American public," said Bill Galston , a senior fellow in governance studies at the Brookings Institution thinktank in Washington.

"In the same way that he ransacked the state of Texas for the very worst senatorial nominee imaginable, now he's done the same thing with the chief of staff position. This is simply outrageous."

articles.title: Republican state lawmakers reported Omar to the IRS in 2019
articles.summary: Years before Omar's latest federal probe, Minnesota Republicans flagged her controversial tax filings to the IRS, according to newly obtained correspondence.
articles.body: EXCLUSIVE: A group of Minnesota Republican state lawmakers asked the IRS in August 2019 to "conduct a detailed reexamination" of tax filings by Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., based on a report from a state board suggesting she filed joint tax returns in 2014 and 2015 with a man she was not legally married to, according to a letter obtained by Fox News Digital. The letter was sent after the Minnesota Campaign Finance and Public Disclosure Board issued a report on June 6, 2019, indicating that Omar had filed joint tax returns in 2014 and 2015 with Ahmed Hirsi, despite being legally married to another man, Ahmed Nur Said Elmi, at the time. The joint tax returns came up during the Minnesota Campaign Finance and Public Disclosure Board’s examination of a $1,500 expense associated with Omar’s campaign committee. The board was investigating whether the expenditure was a legitimate campaign-related expense or whether campaign funds had been used to pay for services that benefited Omar personally. The payment was part of a larger $2,250 reimbursement to the Kjellberg Law Office for legal and other services. ILHAN OMAR ISSUES STUNNING ADMISSION WHEN CONFRONTED WITH BROTHER MARRIAGE RUMORS In response to the board’s questions, Omar’s campaign committee explained that the Kjellberg Law Office had retained the accounting firm Frederick & Rosen to obtain and review financial records as part of the campaign committee’s efforts to respond to allegations surrounding Omar’s marital history. According to the committee’s explanation, Frederick & Rosen prepared releases for Omar and Ahmed Hirsi to sign, so the firm could obtain copies of their filed joint federal income tax returns for 2014 and 2015 from the IRS. The board concluded that the committee had not demonstrated that the $1,500 expense benefited the campaign and required Omar to reimburse the committee. JD VANCE SAYS DOJ LOOKING INTO IF ILHAN OMAR COMMITTED IMMIGRATION FRAUD AMID BROTHER-MARRIAGE ALLEGATIONS Omar married Hirsi in 2002 in their Muslim faith tradition and that they ended their relationship in that tradition in 2008, Newsweek reported. She then legally married Ahmed Nur Said Elmi in February 2009, according to public records, as reported by Newsweek. According to divorce documents obtained by Fox News Digital, Omar legally divorced Elmi in December 2017. Carla Kjellberg, a lawyer for Omar and her campaign committee, stated during the board proceedings that Frederick & Rosen’s services provided "some personal benefit to Rep. Omar," because "there was an issue with her tax returns that needed to be corrected regardless of her status as a candidate," according to the board’s report. In a letter to then-IRS Commissioner Charles Rettig dated Aug. 6, 2019, the state lawmakers asked the IRS to undertake a review in light of the Minnesota Campaign Finance Board report. "Due to recent developments, I believe probable cause exists for an investigation into Rep. Omar's tax filings," read the letter, signed by Minnesota state Reps. Steve Drazkowski, Linda Runbeck, Glenn Gruenhagen, Shane Mekeland, John Poston, Eric Lucero, Duane Quam, Tim Miller, Cal Bahr and Jeremy Munson. Drazkowski told Fox News Digital that the IRS never responded to the request. The IRS did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment. Fox News Digital could not confirm whether the IRS followed through with the lawmakers’ request. Federal tax confidentiality rules generally restrict what the agency can disclose about individual taxpayers. The Minnesota Campaign Finance and Public Disclosure Board issued its findings on June 6, 2019, following two complaints filed by Drazkowski. Although the board required Omar to repay the $1,500 that her campaign had paid the Kjellberg Law Firm for Frederick & Rosen’s services related to the tax returns, it rejected the allegation that this money was payment for Omar’s personal divorce proceeding, in which Kjellberg also represented her. The board also required Omar to repay campaign funds used for certain travel expenses, including trips to Boston, New York and Washington, D.C. Following the board's 2019 findings, Omar said she was "glad" the process was complete and welcomed the board's determination regarding allegations that she had improperly used campaign funds for personal expenses. However, she did not address the portion of the board’s report concerning the joint tax returns she submitted with Hirsi. Omar did not respond to Fox News Digital’s request for comment. In a separate letter obtained by Fox News Digital, the Republican state lawmakers, led by Drazkowski, asked Cynthia Bauerly, then-commissioner of the Minnesota Department of Revenue, in August 2019 to review Omar's joint tax filings. Drazkowski said neither Bauerly nor the Minnesota Department of Revenue responded to the lawmakers' request. The Minnesota Department of Revenue did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment. The letter from the lawmakers urging the state and federal tax reporting agencies to investigate Omar’s joint tax filings came two months after Drazkowski urged Rep. Angie Craig, D-Minn., to refer his concerns about Omar's tax filings to the House Ethics Committee. As previously reported by Fox News Digital, Craig told Drazkowski in a letter that he could submit information himself to the Office of Congressional Ethics (OCE), which was renamed to the Office of Congressional Conduct in 2021. The congressional ethics process allows members of the public and lawmakers to submit information concerning alleged misconduct, although the independent ethics office and the House Committee on Ethics have separate procedures. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP In late October, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said on Fox News that the federal investigation into Omar regarding potential immigration and marriage fraud had been referred to the Department of Justice (DOJ) as a "large case" that targets multiple individuals rather than just one person. The DHS did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment on whether the investigation is looking into the 2014 and 2015 joint tax filings flagged by the state lawmakers in 2019.

articles.title: TIM GRAHAM: The blue wave brought a tidal wave of praise from TV networks
articles.summary: James Talarico's "politics of love" drew soft questions from ABC while CBS gushed over Adam Hamilton's Golden Rule pledge to transform Washington.
articles.body: The broadcast networks energetically predicted doom for the Republicans during the fall campaign. And they got their wish. The dramatic blue wave – with the most dramatic shock coming in Texas – caused a wave of positive coverage. On Wednesday morning, Nov. 4, you might expect any winning candidate who gets interviewed is going to receive soft questioning, a form of congratulations. But you might be a little surprised by the fountains of gush. On ABC, former Clinton press secretary George Stephanopoulos was teeing up Texas Sen.-Elect James Talarico with this: "You said you want to pursue a politics of love. For a lot of Americans who may be hearing you for the first time this morning, spell out what that means." DEM WINS TRUMP-TARGETED TEXAS DISTRICT IN REBUKE OF REPUBLICAN REDISTRICTING SHAKEUP Talarico happily complied: "Yeah, I think we are all tired of this politics of division, this politics of hate, this politics of fear. I’m tired of being pitted against my neighbor. I’m tired of being told to hate my neighbor." It's really annoying when Democrats like Talarico or former President Barack Obama accuse the Republicans of seeking to "divide us" even as they suggest the Republicans are evildoers who only care about billionaires. Campaigns are won by dividing people. That's how it works. Does anyone think ABC, CBS and NBC were practicing a "politics of love" and unity leading up to the elections? Not if they were watching TV. TIM GRAHAM: THREE-TO-ONE NEGATIVE COVERAGE TELLS THE STORY OF NETWORK BIAS Over on "CBS Mornings," the hosts were gushing over Kansas Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton, pastor of a Methodist megachurch. Norah O’Donnell asked, "I know you have promised to bring the biblical Golden Rule to D.C., as you have said, ‘Do unto others as you would have them do unto you.’ Have you been to Washington? That place is pretty cutthroat. How are you going to do that?" Gayle King echoed that, oozing, "so many people are really happy to hear you talk about decency and kindness, pastor, because when we were talking to people, they said they’re sick of ... the vulgarity, the crassness, and you said that — people were very touched to hear yesterday that you start your day on your knees and you’re in prayer." REPUBLICANS SUFFER HISTORIC SENATE UPSET AS DEM FLIPS DEEP-RED STATE FOR FIRST TIME IN NEARLY A CENTURY Nate Burleson rounded out the lovefest: "Senator-elect, that was beautiful — being a vessel for the Lord and also being a bridge for the people. Well, let’s talk about it because it’s time to get to work. So, I guess I’ll ask you about the genesis of your work and then what the revelations will be later." When the professing Christians are Democrats, suddenly religion is a wonderful thing. Laugh when they claim the new Editor-in-Chief Bari Weiss has changed the tone of CBS. Speaking of religion, Michigan’s Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed was promoted as the first Muslim to be elected to the Senate, and the networks all read from the same song sheet that he was attacked by Republicans for "his faith." Forget the campaigning with podcaster Hasan "America Deserved 9/11" Piker, or El-Sayed signing a petition calling for a purging of the media in Egypt by the Muslim Brotherhood. It was just cartooned into ignorant prejudice, an Islamophobic attack on Muslims. They touted how he overcame it to make history: FIRST MUSLIM SENATOR, FIRST BLACK FEMALE GOVERNOR: 2026 MIDTERM ELECTION RESULTS MAKE HISTORY ABC’s Mary Bruce: "Abdul El-Sayed becoming the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate after President Trump launched Islamophobic attacks on his faith." CBS’s Nikole Killion: "Abdul el-Sayed is making history this morning as the first Muslim ever elected to the U.S. Senate. In his speech overnight, he shot back at his critics, including his GOP opponent, Mike Rogers. He said this was one of the ugliest campaigns he’s been in and accused his opposition of trying to divide voters by mocking his name and his faith." CBS NEWS TAKES HEAT OVER REPORT ON DEM HOPEFUL ABDUL EL-SAYED'S NOW-DELETED 9/11 POSTS NBC’s Ryan Nobles: The Democrat won "after a bitter and contentious campaign Republicans accusing El-Sayed of anti-Semitism after his criticism of Israel and the Democrat facing personal attacks over his faith, including from President Trump." It's really annoying when Democrats like Talarico or former President Barack Obama accuse the Republicans of seeking to "divide us" even as they suggest the Republicans are evildoers who only care about billionaires. Liz Landers on PBS: "He'll become the first Muslim ever elected to the Senate and withstanding ugly campaign attacks on his faith, including when the president called him a jihadist." DEM AG PULLS OFF UPSET OF SITTING REPUBLICAN GOVERNOR AFTER BLISTERING CAMPAIGN IN KEY SWING STATE Speaking of making history in terms of diversity, on Wipeout Wednesday night’s "PBS News Hour," anchor Geoff Bennett celebrated his list of electoral "historic firsts," but his recap left out Florida electing its first Black governor – perhaps because Byron Donalds is a Republican. They highlighted radical socialist Melat Kiros of Colorado as the "first Generation Z woman elected to Congress," but not the Black governors, which also included Democrats Aaron Ford in Nevada and David Crowley in Wisconsin. Piker proclaimed that "virtually every locality, every state, every House district decided to punish the Trump administration and the Republican Party for the death and destruction it's brought about all around the world." articles.title: Healthcare, economy top Democrat priorities after midterms
articles.summary: (The Center Square) - With Democrats taking control of Congress in 2027, leaders and advocates are calling for meaningful reforms to healthcare and policies...
articles.body:
(The Center Square) - With Democrats taking control of Congress in 2027, leaders and advocates are calling for meaningful reforms to healthcare and policies that prioritize affordability.

Across the country, Democrats won sweeping victories in what is considered a rebuke of high gas and other prices amid the U.S. military conflict in Iran and President Donald Trump's sinking approval rating.

Some Democratic leaders are calling for a focus on legislation that addresses affordability concerns and a shift away from partisanship. Rebecca Perkins Kwoka, leader of New Hampshire's Senate Democrats, said lawmakers in the state would not focus on abortion expansion or marijuana legalization, rather on economic issues.

"We are focused on lowering costs and making sure that there are no distractions in the statehouse from doing the work the voters have asked us to do," Kwoka said on a press call with The Center Square. "This is housing, childcare, lowering healthcare costs, lowering energy costs, lowering property taxes."

One area where advocates have called for Democrats to pay attention is healthcare. In January, work requirements in the One Big Beautiful Bill will take effect, removing individuals from healthcare plans who do not align with the new work standards.

Casey Hite, CEO of Aeroflow Health, said most people are not aware about the extent to which they will lose healthcare coverage. Aerflow found 71% of members were concerned about the change to eligibility requirements and accidental coverage loss.

"The best case is that those requirements can be delayed, but time will tell," Hite told The Center Square in an interview. "The election changed who holds the gavel, it doesn't change the calendar."

Hite said he is concerned that states across the country will not collect accurate information for Medicaid recipients to verify eligibility in federal healthcare programs.

"We're going to have people losing coverage that shouldn't otherwise lose coverage," Hite warned.

Democrats are expected to face challenges when governing with a broad coalition. Erin Covey, an analyst at The Cook Political Report, highlighted the potential divide between Democratic Socialists of America candidates and moderate Democrats heading to Congress.

"I do think that [DSA members] were able to tap into a frustration with the system that a lot of more moderate establishment Democrats were a little bit slower to get on board with, but did by the time we kind of got into the general election," Covey said.

Texas state Rep. Salman Bhojani said data centers will be a key focus for Democrats throughout the state in the upcoming year. Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa focused on this issue throughout her campaign while data center development exploded in the state.

"My goal is to govern from the middle, not swing left or swing right, and give Republicans a seat at the table," Bhojani said in a news conference. "Even though we don't need them, I think we need to give a seat at the table, and because policy comes from both sides of the aisle. So I look forward to governing in the near future."

Hite emphasized the importance of bipartisan healthcare policy moving forward in Congress. He projected optimism about legislation Democrats can work on in collaboration with President Donald Trump that will provide relief to patients across the country.

"The president knows how important healthcare is. He's got two more years in office, he has a legacy that he wants to maintain and buttress," Hite said. "He might very well sign legislation, if it makes sense."

Trump has declared himself "Mr. Veto" while referring to his power to block legislation passed by Congress. As it stands, Democrats do not have enough votes in Congress to overcome a presidential veto.

Iowa Sen. Matt Blake said he would take the same bipartisan approach in the state legislature, after Democrats flipped the governorship and the Iowa House in the traditionally red state.

"We will be part of a working coalition of split government here, where we're going to work across the aisle, work with Republicans and work with Democrats to try to find solutions for Iowans, covering issues that others have talked about: data centers, affordability, we're going to tackle those," Blake said.

articles.title: What Stephen Miller has pushed for while in Trump administration
articles.summary: Top Trump adviser Stephen Miller, who is set to take over the White House chief of staff role on Monday, has driven President Trump's most controversial immi...
articles.body:
Washington — Top Trump adviser Stephen Miller , who is set to take over the White House chief of staff role on Monday, has driven President Trump's most controversial immigration policies during both of his administrations.

Mr. Trump announced the staffing shake-up on Friday, calling Miller one of his "most trusted" advisers. Miller replaces Susie Wiles, who has been his chief of staff throughout his second term.

The move comes after Republicans suffered crippling losses in the midterm elections and as Democrats plan sweeping investigations into the administration's actions, including its immigration enforcement policies.

Miller was the architect behind many of those policies and also championed the administration's immigration enforcement expansion, which has been supported by approximately $170 billion that congressional Republicans allocated for immigration enforcement and border security in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which became law in July 2025.

During Mr. Trump's first term, Miller helped develop and publicly defend the administration's executive order that restricted entry by nationals of several Muslim-majority countries. The travel ban led to protests around the U.S. and legal challenges. A third iteration of the ban was upheld by the Supreme Court in 2018.

He was a leading supporter of the administration's 2018 zero-tolerance immigration policy, which resulted in thousands of family separations, and he pressed for dramatic reductions in refugee admissions. The administration repeatedly lowered the annual refugee admissions ceiling, ultimately setting it at 15,000 for fiscal year 2021, a record low at the time. Under former President Barack Obama, the ceiling was 110,000 for fiscal year 2017.

Miller also advocated penalizing legal immigrants who received public benefits and making it harder for them to obtain citizenship.

In Mr. Trump's second term, Miller pushed Immigration and Customs Enforcement to make at least 3,000 immigration arrests per day. In May 2025, Miller publicly demanded a dramatic increase in daily arrests, placing pressure on ICE leadership and expanding enforcement beyond immigrants who had been convicted of serious crimes.

He also proposed that the National Guard be deployed to support mass deportations.

Miller's arrest targets were part of a sweeping expansion of enforcement in communities, workplaces and immigration courts. Detentions of immigrants without criminal histories rose sharply , and increased ICE activity sparked protests across the country.

The longtime Trump adviser also championed the use of a wartime law — the Alien Enemies Act of 1798 — to bypass due process and quickly deport alleged Venezuelan gang members to El Salvador, where they were held in a notorious maximum-security prison, known as CECOT. The deportations set off a legal battle, and the Supreme Court blocked the government from immediately deporting the Venezuelans without giving them an opportunity to challenge their removal.

As part of the administration's deportation efforts, Miller has supported an aggressive expansion of third-country deportations . The administration has deported immigrants to countries where they have no citizenship or family ties, including several African nations .

In May 2025, Miller said the administration was actively considering suspending the constitutional mechanism that allows detainees to challenge their confinement in court.

At a March 2026 conference in Miami, Miller argued that military force, rather than traditional criminal law enforcement alone, was needed to defeat cartels.

Miller appeared alongside Mr. Trump in the Oval Office this summer as he signed executive orders to refuse citizenship to some children born in the United States, after the Supreme Court struck down his earlier executive order aiming to end birthright citizenship.

articles.title: Trump officials weigh major overhaul of National Park Service, Fish and Wildlife
articles.summary: The Interior Department is considering an overhaul of the National Park Service, internal documents show, possibly mirroring steps already taken at the U.S....
articles.body:
The Trump administration is considering a major reorganization of the National Park Service and the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, according to internal documents reviewed by The Washington Post.

Staff are meeting this week and next to discuss a "realignment" of the two agencies, the documents show. One meeting regarding the National Park Service will discuss "pending duty station changes," referring to the locations where staff report to work. But the documents do not specify whether certain offices would be closed or moved, or whether any employees would be fired.

The Interior Department, which oversees the agencies, did not respond to a request for comment.

News and guidance on climate, science and technology. Sign up for free

Public land advocates fear that the changes could further hurt agencies that have already seen major staffing cuts since Trump began efforts to shrink the federal government by hundreds of thousands of employees last year.

"I think from their perspective, it seems as though that they're trying to find efficiencies by consolidating staff within DOI that maybe served different functions across these agencies," said Ed Stierli, vice president of government affairs at the National Parks Conservation Association, an advocacy group. "But I think in reality, it just seems to be causing more confusion and chaos. "

While the administration has considered differing plans to overhaul the Park Service since last year, including one reported in September by the Washington Sun, plans to reorganize the Fish and Wildlife Service are more recent. Fish and Wildlife manages more than 500 National Wildlife Refuges across the country, spanning 93 million acres.

A Fish and Wildlife Service report published on Friday recommends the agency "reduce headquarters and regional office staffing and reallocate positions to refuge operations, prioritizing the people needed to manage habitat, maintain facilities, support public access and protect resources."

An internal communication to Fish and Wildlife Service staff on Friday, reviewed by The Post, states that the recommendations in the report "give us a path forward" and that "our next responsibility is to turn them into practical actions."

In March, the administration initiated a reorganization of the U.S. Forest Service, which includes relocating its headquarters from Washington to Salt Lake City and hundreds of employees with it. The plan would also close some research stations and regional offices as it transitions to state offices.

A judge has put that plan on hold , as well as a wider reorganization of the Agriculture Department that oversees it, amid legal challenges.

At the Park Service, the administration has withheld millions in funding and cut Park Service staff by about a quarter, sometimes leading to long lines, fewer tours and dirty bathrooms at parks.

"When you talk about changing duty stations for example, are they just trying to cripple this agency?" Stierli asked. "Why would you try and sow chaos into an agency that is already stretched well beyond capacity trying to fulfill its mission?"

Bill Wade, executive director of the Association of National Park Rangers, which represents current and former Park Service employees, said that agency employees have had to live with the uncertainty and stress that major restructuring might be coming, possibly including layoffs, since the launch of the DOGE Service last year.

Based on the limited information about the current reorganization being considered, "it's too little to try to determine what the impact would be on the service or employees," Wade said.

It is unclear whether the current reorganization plans for the National Park Service had been significantly revised from earlier proposals. Layoff plans last year at the National Park Service, which have not been independently verified by The Post, were ultimately never carried out.

Stierli said that the administration appeared to "pump the brakes" on the plans two months ago, but it may now be feeling a new sense of urgency to restructure the agency with Democrats about to take control of Congress.

"Come January, you're going have a new Congress who's very eager to do oversight and pry into the National Park Service to look and see how staff are being organized, where is the budget for the Park Service going," Stierli said.

In spending bills, congressional Democrats could write in provisions demanding approval over any restructuring in agencies, or at least to be notified, he said.

"We're certainly hopeful that Congress uses this oversight power here, because I think what's highly unusual is there's been zero transparency," Stierli added. "When there is zero transparency, it creates this confusion."

articles.title: Trump ally Loomer was paid thousands for political tweets, people familiar say
articles.summary: The right-wing activist Laura Loomer has been paid by private clients to make political posts on social media without publicly disclosing the payments, accor...
articles.body:
The right-wing activist Laura Loomer has been paid by private clients to make political posts on social media without publicly disclosing the payments, according to a former campaign aide to President Donald Trump and three others familiar with the arrangements, shedding light on what they say is a business practice of one of the Trump administration's most influential online firebrands.

The allegations were made by Alex Bruesewitz, an adviser to Trump's 2024 campaign, and three other people who spoke on the condition of anonymity. Two of the three people said they had paid Loomer directly to post political messages on her X account, where she has 1.9 million followers. The third said they had overseen clients who paid her to post on the account. The three spoke on the condition of anonymity.

Bank transaction emails and a wire transfer statement reviewed by The Washington Post appear to show four payments totaling more than $60,000 sent to Loomer and a Florida-based company registered in her name, King Breaker Media, since May of last year.

The documents do not specify the purpose of the payments, but two people familiar with the arrangements said they were for political posts.

Loomer, one of Trump's best-known online acolytes, denied to The Post that she is paid to post on social media. She instead described herself as a journalist and activist and disputed the idea that she is an influencer paid to promote any political cause.

The new claims about Loomer's influence business could add fuel to a growing debate about the little-regulated industry of political messaging on social media, where influencers on both sides of the aisle have operated in a legal gray area between advocacy and advertising.

Bruesewitz first posted his allegations on X on Thursday. Many of the details about Loomer's alleged online influence operation have not been previously reported.

Bruesewitz said in an interview with The Post that he had paid Loomer for tweets last year. He said the money had been sent through his political consulting firm, X Strategies, for posts related to policy issues. He declined to specify what clients.

Despite brokering these deals himself, he believes that they should require clearer disclosures and have "gotten out of hand."

Loomer disputed Bruesewitz's account and said that his firm contacted her last year offering to pay her for research.

"He paid me to make a one-page research document for him, and then he wanted me to distribute the information. And that's what I did," Loomer said. Asked where she was expected to distribute the research, she said, "Either X or maybe an article."

When asked how that was different from being paid to tweet, Loomer said she had actually been told to create the research document but that Bruesewitz had said he would have it distributed.

Loomer accused Bruesewitz of "lashing out" at her because of her political beliefs.

Bruesewitz and the three other people declined to publicly share the tweets they said Loomer had published to maintain the privacy of their clients. But The Post reviewed a selection of the tweets under the condition that they not be revealed publicly.

Two of the people said that Loomer charges $3,000 to $5,000 per tweet, and sometimes more.

Loomer said she does not have set pricing for consulting work. "I certainly don't charge $5,000 for a tweet," she said.

The four people who had paid or oversaw payments to Loomer for posting political statements on social media said she is an effective, if sometimes unpredictable, messenger and a key way of trying to get a line directly to Trump.

Jared Holt, a senior researcher at Open Measures, a platform that measures the spread of online extremism and disinformation, agreed. "This is somebody that has a tremendous amount of influence and access to the president's ear," said Holt, who studies the far right.

Loomer said in an interview Thursday night that she could not discuss the terms of her work with most of her clients due to confidentiality agreements and the fact that her accountant handled her invoices.

"I'm not some influencer that makes money from tweeting. My business is public affairs and opposition research," she said. "I also have a media company. It's not illegal to make a living in America."

Roughly one hour after The Post discussed the claims with Loomer, she announced on X that she is taking a hiatus from her online show, "Loomer Unleashed," so she could pursue a more "healthy work life balance" and prepare for her upcoming wedding.

"I just need to step back, recharge, refocus, and be present in my own life and my own mind with peace and clarity for a little while," she wrote. Loomer said the announcement had been scheduled in advance.

Loomer, 33, has traveled with Trump and met privately with him in the Oval Office during his second term in office. Detractors within the administration have taken issue with Loomer's relationship to the president and have lamented that several high-ranking defense and national security officials have been dismissed after she has publicly rebuked them, often on her X account.

Trump last year called Loomer a "very nice person" and a "patriot." After the White House fired aides on the National Security Council staff last year whom Loomer had accused of disloyalty, Trump denied that she was involved in the dismissal but acknowledged she had made some firing recommendations and said, "Sometimes I listen to those recommendations."

The Federal Trade Commission requires bloggers, influencers and other online figures to disclose when they have been paid to endorse a product, but the agency doesn't have jurisdiction over political ads.

Some advocacy groups have called for stronger regulations around paid political content. The Campaign Legal Center last year petitioned the Federal Election Commission to consider requiring "paid for by" disclosures on influencers' political posts, saying they could help voters better assess the content they see online. California Gov. Gavin Newsom recently signed legislation that will penalize influencers who post paid political messages without disclosure.

The general lack of transparency among political influencers, Holt said, "further degrades confidence in what people see online and how genuine it may be, or how representative it may actually be of the communities that these various influencers purport to speak for."

Loomer has frequently said her bulldog advocacy reflects her genuine views, telling The Bulwark in May 2025 that she was "not paid for [her] posts."

One person who said they had paid Loomer to tweet on behalf of clients said she was deliberate in her work and would only tweet if she agreed with the position. The person said not every client wanted to work with her because they believed she was polarizing but that some had hired her assuming she had an audience in the White House.

The person added, however, that Loomer was like a "nuclear bomb." "You have to be careful how to use that," they said. "It's effective but also turns a lot of things to s--- if you're not careful."

Loomer said she took that as a compliment. "I'm glad people find me to be effective and think I have a good reach," she said. "I'm not going to apologize for monetizing the fact that people fear me."

articles.title: The ascendency of JD Vance
articles.summary: The Republican Party failed “Working Class 101” on Tuesday, to the sustained glee of the Democratic Party. Will the GOP learn its lesson before 2028?
articles.body:
Almost every Republican I speak with strongly agrees with the “Blue Tsunami” post authored by Vice President JD Vance in the wake of the Republicans’ midterm defeat. “The real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone,” he said. “The reason we lost is the war.”

Although I enthusiastically endorse that reasoning, it remains essential that the so-called braintrust of the Republican Party — it’s difficult not to snicker at that label after Tuesday’s political annihilation — understand why the fallout of that war was political kryptonite for Republicans.

First and foremost, it’s having a massive negative impact on the working class of our nation — a constituency that, according to a recent PEW survey , makes up 60 percent of adults in our nation. In other words, the majority of voters in the U.S. are working class.

But does anyone in authority within the Trump administration personally know anyone from the working class? Do they think about these people at all while toasting their spoils in cryptocurrency, data centers and soon to be built luxury resorts?

Yes, that’s perhaps a bit snarky. But it may be well-deserved when one stops to think about the fact that nine in 10 voters identified the cost of living as a major concern long before Tuesday’s election. Paycheck-to-paycheck voters saw that concern morph into a punishing reality as the war with Iran caused a continuous spike in the price of gasoline, diesel fuel, groceries and basic commodities.

For decades, most Americans identified the Democratic Party as the party of blue-collar Americans. Then, as the party increasingly became more infatuated with elites and Big Tech, the Trump-Vance campaign swooped in and successfully co-opted the blue-collar mantle.

But this year, as the Trump administration prioritized the will of neocons and their push for war over the needs of the people, that script was flipped again. So much so that if one listened to the victory speeches delivered Tuesday night with your eyes closed, you would swear you were hearing talking points from the Reagan era promoting the commonsense ideals that speak to all in the working class.

To the surprise of no one, Republicans ceded much of that vote back to the Democrats on Tuesday evening. As United Auto Workers President Shawn Fain put it on Wednesday: “I say this all the time: Look, we’re not Republicans, we are not Democrats, we aren’t independents. We support people that back us.”

As Republicans wrestle with that issue, the party has another major problem on its hands: Gen Z. As poll after poll indicated, a whopping seven out of 10 voters under the age of 30 just voted for the Democrats.

That is not an implosion. That is a death knell.

Could it be that no one in the administration knows anyone from that generation, beyond their own nepo-babies and rich kids, who is struggling to pay the bills, increasingly pessimistic that they will never, ever realize the American dream that was promised to them? If they did, they would know that there are millions of such Gen Z citizens out there currently scared out of their minds.

If the Republicans hope to have any chance to keep the White House and claw back some House and Senate seats come 2028, they are going to need a new champion — someone who has an ear pre-tuned to the working class, the disenfranchised and the youth vote.

Vance knows the pain of those communities because he lived their lives. He is not a nepo-baby. He did not grow up rich. More than that, at just 42 years of age, with four young children, Vance is closer to the Gen Z demographic than almost anyone else in authority within the administration.

As the post-mortems continue for the Republicans, it would be wise to recognize that a sea-change is desperately needed. It is time to cede more control of the political machine to Vance and his team. Sooner or later, all political batons must be handed off if victory is to be attained.

The blue-collar vote has flipped back to the Democrats for the moment. For the Republican Party, it’s either listen, learn, acknowledge and empathize, evolve or perish.

Douglas MacKinnon is a former White House and Pentagon official.

articles.title: Trump’s glide path to judicial confirmations comes to an end
articles.summary: Democrats’ Senate victory means President Trump for the first time will lose a glide path to nominate judges and Supreme Court justices. Pressure had grown on conservative Justices Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito to retire, but they show no sign of imminently stepping down. And Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (N.Y.) is already signaling…
articles.body:
Democrats’ Senate victory means President Trump for the first time will lose a glide path to nominate judges and Supreme Court justices.

Pressure had grown on conservative Justices Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito to retire, but they show no sign of imminently stepping down.

And Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (N.Y.) is already signaling the party, burned by past confirmation fights, could be a roadblock if a Supreme Court vacancy ever arises in the new Congress.

“The bottom line is we’re not going to allow a right-winger on the court,” Schumer told The Associated Press in an interview.

It’s a major shift in dynamics after Trump’s remaking of the federal courts became one of his most lasting first-term legacies.

He nominated dozens of lower court judges and three justices to the Supreme Court — Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett — to cement its 6-3 conservative majority.

That legacy carried over to the lower courts, too. By this point in his first term, the Senate had confirmed 83 of Trump’s judicial nominees, according to Federal Judicial Center data.

With Democrats set to take over the Senate majority and the chamber’s advice and consent power on the president’s nominees in a matter of weeks, a continued climb is increasingly in jeopardy. And the confirmation pace was already slower this term, with 56 confirmed so far, according to the data.

It’s left some Republicans calling for a swift push on the remaining lower court openings before the new Congress begins in January.

“Every single federal judicial vacancy needs to be filled in the lame duck session,” Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) wrote on social media Friday . “The Senate should pull all-nighters for as long as it takes. Democrats wont confirm a single Trump judge once they take over.”

Twenty-eight district court vacancies are waiting to be filled, with nominees pending for 11 of them, according to the federal judiciary’s administrative office.

Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier (R) called on the Senate to confirm U.S. district court nominee Robert Long, saying he’s one of the “finest jurists” and lamenting that his nomination has been pending for months.

Mike Davis, a close legal ally of the president, ramped up pressure on Arkansas’s Republican senators — Tom Cotton and John Boozman — to confirm Lee Rudofsky to an appeals court seat. Rudofsky serves in a trial judgeship in Arkansas, and Davis accused the senators of having “wanted someone else.”

“They need to change their minds–and fast–or Republicans will lose this key appellate court seat,” Davis wrote on social platform X .

Spokespeople for Cotton and Boozman did not return a request for comment.

The president appears set to continue announcing new names as the lame-duck session begins. James Sullivan, who is projected to lose his seat on the Texas Supreme Court in this week’s elections, is set to be nominated to a federal judgeship, according to a questionnaire submitted to the Senate this week first reported by Reuters.

The midterms have also shifted the political dynamics for Supreme Court vacancies.

In Trump’s first term, Democrats accused Republicans of stealing Supreme Court seats for Gorsuch and Barrett. They voted against Kavanaugh over sexual assault accusations that he denies. But Democrats never had the votes to block the nominations after Republicans eliminated the filibuster for Supreme Court nominees. Now, Democrats are expressing glee with the party projected to win at least 54 Senate seats, including in red states like Texas, Kansas and South Carolina. Depending on how the races in Alaska and Mississippi shake out, the party could ultimately win as many as 56 seats heading into the new Congress.

Some outside pressure had grown on Thomas, 78, and Alito, 76, the court’s two oldest conservative justices, to step down ahead of the election to ensure Trump could send a replacement while the Senate remained under Republicans’ control.

Many of those voices pointed to the late liberal Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, who remained on the court despite liberal pressure until her 2020 death, enabling Trump to replace her just days before the presidential election.

As pressure grew on Alito and Thomas, others on the right condemned the talk. Leonard Leo, the judicial activist who played a central role in the Supreme Court’s conservative shift, publicly called the retirement speculation “crass.” Even Trump put the talk to the side.

“I hope they stay, ’cause I think they’re fantastic, OK?” Trump said last year .

Ultimately, Alito told CBS News in an interview that aired last month that he “thought about” stepping down but decided against it.

“It’s something I think that somebody at my age has to think about every term. But I thought that I could still make a valuable contribution, which is why I became a justice and a judge in the first place,” he said.

Following Democrats’ win, Alito has again told people he does not plan to immediately step down, according to reports from The New York Times and Bloomberg . Alito did not return The Hill’s request for comment about his plans.

Thomas, meanwhile, recently became the second-longest-serving justice in American history. Many court watchers expect he’ll set the record — a feat he’ll reach in May 2028.

Although they are the court’s oldest members at 78 and 76, respectively, Thomas and Alito are still younger than recent justices who’ve retired.

Justice Stephen Breyer served until he was nearly 84. Justice Anthony Kennedy had just turned 82 on his last day. Before him, Justice John Paul Stevens served until age 90.

The most recent justice to retire younger than the duo’s ages was Justice David Souter, who stepped down in 2009 at the age of 69 to return to a quieter life in New Hampshire.

articles.title: What Trump shares with Truman after a midterm shellacking
articles.summary: Shortly after World War II, as the United States faced a rising Soviet Union, a devastated Europe, and the dawn of a Cold War, President Harry S. Truman got...
articles.body:
Brett McGurk is a CNN global affairs analyst who served in senior national security positions under Presidents George W. Bush, Barack Obama, Donald Trump and Joe Biden. He is the author of Brink : Inside the Race to Free the October 7 Hostages.

Shortly after World War II, as the United States faced a rising Soviet Union, a devastated Europe, and the dawn of a Cold War, President Harry S. Truman's Democratic Party got clobbered in midterm elections.

In 1946, Republicans gained 55 seats in the House and 12 in the Senate, taking control of both chambers for the first time in 16 years.

Truman's presidency seemed finished. One senator from his own party, J. William Fulbright of Arkansas, suggested that Truman appoint a Republican secretary of state and resign, handing over the presidency under the succession law then in effect.

Truman turned to Senator Arthur Vandenberg, a former isolationist from Michigan who became chairman of the Foreign Relations Committee in the new Congress.

Their unlikely partnership helped produce the Truman Doctrine, the Marshall Plan, and ultimately the North Atlantic Treaty establishing NATO. Together, they helped build a strategy that contained Soviet expansion and laid the groundwork for winning the Cold War decades later.

Vandenberg's guiding principle: partisan politics should stop "at the water's edge."

The two men continued fighting. Truman campaigned against the "do-nothing" Republican Congress. Vandenberg was still a Republican with presidential ambitions.

But they agreed on the challenges confronting the United States and found ways to work together where it most mattered for the country.

Eighty years later, that seems almost unimaginable.

Trump now faces a predicament Truman would recognize: a midterm shellacking that handed both houses of Congress to the opposition.

We are in a technology race with China over artificial intelligence — and with it the future of economic and military power. Europe faces the risk of a larger war as Russia's invasion of Ukraine nears the five-year mark. The US is mired in a stalemate with Iran with no easy exit and no reason to expect Tehran to abandon its hostility toward America, support for terrorism, or nuclear ambitions.

All these threats will outlast Trump's presidency. Each requires decisions now that may take years or decades to bear fruit. And each becomes harder when Washington cannot sustain a policy long enough to make it work.

Consider the view from the other side of the ocean.

If you are Vladimir Putin, why compromise if America is divided and its support for Ukraine might collapse first? The same goes for China's president, Xi Jinping, who views the United States as riven with divisions and in terminal decline.

Or Iran's leaders: why compromise when the United States might soon abandon the Middle East altogether? Mojtaba Khamenei, Iran's new Supreme Leader —albeit one who has never been seen — seemed to speak for all three when he said "the US's collapse has accelerated" after the midterms.

Even here at home, if you are an American manufacturer being asked to expand weapons production, why build a factory without confidence that Washington will purchase what it produces?

Call it the price of uncertainty. Adversaries press advantage. Allies hedge. American industry holds back.

The Truman–Vandenberg partnership worked because both men accepted responsibilities that went beyond efforts to defeat the other party.

Truman had a theory of the case: Soviet expansion threatened American security, and the US needed to strengthen countries vulnerable to Soviet pressure.

The Marshall Plan supplied economic means. The emerging Atlantic alliance supplied military means. Bipartisan congressional support gave both durability.

Truman also accepted that Vandenberg would help shape the policy.

His administration consulted the senator as proposals developed. Vandenberg demanded changes and brought skeptical Republicans along. He took responsibility for policies because he had helped design them.

There is a lesson here for both parties today.

A partnership for the good of the country requires political trade-offs. The president must accept that his legacy now requires working with Democrats, who must in turn accept that a policy worth supporting might also give Trump a win.

Neither comes naturally in Washington today. Neither came naturally in Truman's Washington, either.

To be sure, a similar partnership today is unlikely, but the need for one is no less urgent. And it's not impossible to envision.

Senator Chris Coons of Delaware is expected to chair the Foreign Relations Committee. Representative Gregory Meeks of New York is positioning to lead its House counterpart. I have worked with both across administrations. Both are deeply experienced and able to forge compromises where necessary with the White House. And both understand the responsibilities involved and represent pragmatic wings of their party.

They would face resistance from Democrats who see the election result as a mandate for two years of confrontation with Trump — not cooperation. But the new Congress can still exercise its oversight and hold Trump to account while pursuing bipartisan deals in foreign affairs.

Trump presents the more fundamental obstacle. A congressional partner needs to know what he is being asked to support — and whether the president will support it tomorrow. Consistency and shared ownership are hardly Trump's political instincts.

But presume a Truman–Vandenberg spirit. What could be accomplished?

On Ukraine, a multiyear agreement might sustain military, economic, and intelligence support, ask more of European partners, and expand American weapons production to replenish our stocks at scale.

On China, an agreement might accelerate the energy and computing infrastructure needed to win the AI race while addressing electricity costs and economic disruption.

On Iran, Trump launched a war without clear objectives or an endpoint. A cooperative approach might define objectives, benchmarks, and a strategy to wind down the conflict while containing Iran and preventing it from rebuilding its nuclear program.

In each case, a president forced to define objectives and reconcile aims with resources produces better and more lasting policies.

The election divided responsibility for governing. It did not suspend the challenges confronting the United States. Those challenges may accelerate as enemies seek advantage and friends hedge against a Washington treading water until another election.

That was the danger in 1946, as well. Truman and Vandenberg gave other countries — friend and foe alike — reason to believe American commitments would survive American elections.

To be sure, Trump would have to offer coherent strategies and accept a congressional role in shaping them. Democratic leaders would have to accept responsibility for making them work.

The alternative is to spend two years proving to foes that they can outlast us—and to friends that they should make other plans.

For more CNN news and newsletters create an account at CNN.com

articles.title: Judge wants former US attorney to investigate whether the government misled her in Trump golf case
articles.summary: WASHINGTON (AP) — A federal judge said Saturday she intends to appoint an ex-top federal prosecutor in the nation's capital during President Donald Trump's f...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — A federal judge said Saturday she intends to appoint an ex-top federal prosecutor in the nation's capital during President Donald Trump's first term to investigate whether she was purposefully misled by lawyers and administration officials in a lawsuit challenging one of his prized Washington construction projects, the renovation of a historic public golf course along the Potomac River.

Jessie Liu, a former U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia, would examine whether officials with the Interior Department and the National Park Service and attorneys with the Department of Justice violated ethics or misled U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes during the course of the case that was initiated in February by the DC Preservation League and two golfers.

The Republican administration plans to close the East Potomac Golf Course and park on Nov. 15 with the intention of constructing a "World Class, championship-level golf course that is capable of hosting major events." An injunction issued by Reyes last month temporarily bars the government from removing or damaging any additional trees on the course and the administration must give 10 days' notice in writing before making any "irreparable modification" to any "forms or features" of the course while the lawsuit is active.

Reyes is giving each side a chance to be heard on her plan to name Liu as special master in the case. They must do so in writing by Friday, when the next court hearing in the dispute is scheduled.

Reyes, who was nominated by Democratic President Joe Biden, wants to know whether federal officials lied about the extent of renovation plans during months of hearings. She also wants to know if they were truthful about various steps they took, including cutting hundreds of trees early last month. She announced during a hearing Oct. 30 that she was starting a formal investigation of the government's conduct. Earlier in the case, she had rejected numerous motions from the plaintiffs to step in, saying she trusted the government attorneys.

As the city's chief federal prosecutor, Liu oversaw some of the matters referred to her office by then-special counsel Robert Mueller during his investigation into possible ties between Trump's 2016 campaign and Russia. Trump later nominated her to be associate attorney general, the third-highest ranking Justice Department job.

Liu withdrew from consideration after running into opposition on the Republican-led Senate Judiciary Committee because of her past membership in a lawyers' group that has supported abortion rights. She eventually resigned from the group because, she said previously, it took left-leaning positions, and she is now part of her own law firm, Liu Shur Kravis LLP.

David Super, a law professor at the Georgetown University Law Center, said the initiation of a formal investigation by a judge to look into the conduct of a trial's participants "can be a precursor to holding someone in contempt of court."

Super said it also is a reflection "of the difficulty she had in determining who initiated the tree-cutting in defiance of the assurances DOJ provided. She doesn't have the time to keep holding long, complex hearings and so wants a special master to narrow the issues."

Reyes ordered the Oct. 30 hearing after multiple Truth Social posts by Trump indicated there were plans for the golf course and construction was expected to begin Nov. 15. Trump said the park would be closed for 15 months while work goes on.

The presidential posts, which began Oct. 18, created a tense dynamic in multiple court hearings afterward when administration officials could not confirm the existence of the plans under questioning from Reyes. She eventually asked whom she should trust. The Justice Department filed notice Oct. 28 that the plans were real.

articles.title: Trump stands by Hegseth as GOP criticism mounts and he pushes to restart the Iran war
articles.summary: The U.S. defense secretary is facing intense political backlash over the costly and unpopular war with Iran, which the president acknowledged was partly to b...
articles.body:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is facing intense political backlash over the United States' costly and unpopular war with Iran following the historic drubbing Republicans took from Democrats in this week's midterm elections. But President Trump has said he is not considering replacing his Pentagon chief, at least not yet.

"No, I think he's doing a very good job," Trump told reporters. On Thursday, Trump said Hegseth had "done a fantastic job," Reuters reported .

The president also said he was unaware of a report that Hegseth has been quietly angling to fill the U.S. Senate seat that will be vacated by Tennessee GOP Sen. Marsha Blackburn, who was elected as the state's next governor this week.

"I think he's doing a very good job, and I actually think he'd be very popular if he did that. But I haven't heard that at all," Trump said when asked if he would want the defense secretary to fill Blackburn's seat.

According to CBS News , though, Trump "has been asking advisers" whether Hegseth should stay or go. The White House has denied reports that Hegseth would leave his job in a post-election shake-up, the BBC reported . The Pentagon has said Hegseth is "100 percent committed" to serving through the end of Trump's term.

Hegseth, a former Fox News host who has served as defense secretary since January 2025, has been Trump's most visible cheerleader for the Iran war, which the U.S. and Israel initiated in February and which has led to surging oil prices.

Hegseth has also been among the advisers urging Trump to restart the war. He and Adm. Brad Cooper, the head of U.S. Central Command, have supported a return to major combat operations against Iran during recent briefings on military options, The Wall Street Journal reported Friday, citing U.S. officials. Vice President JD Vance and special envoy Steve Witkoff have pushed for diplomacy to end the conflict, the Journal reported.

Trump acknowledged Wednesday that the Iran war had partly contributed to the midterm election rout that handed Democrats control of Congress. Vance was unequivocal.

"The real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone," Vance wrote in a lengthy post on X . "The reason we lost is the war."

The vice president did not call out Hegseth by name. But other Republicans did.

Sen. Thom Tillis, a Republican from North Carolina, told CBS News that Hegseth faces "a reckoning."

"He is one of the reasons why we don't have the funding or guarantee for defense that we need," Tillis said on election night. "I think after the election, we need to determine whether or not he's the best person to bring those needs to Congress."

Tillis, who voted to confirm Hegseth last year, recently called on Trump to fire him.

"I have never witnessed more inept management of the brave men and women who serve our country," Tillis wrote in a scathing assessment of Hegseth on X in September. "He is intimidated by competence and retreats to ginning up culture wars instead of soberly attending to the vital work of our national defense and the health and well-being of our fighting force. I urge the President to find a new leader at the Pentagon who will retain and empower our military talent rather than diminish it."

Rep. James Comer of Kentucky, the Republican chairman of the House Oversight Committee, said Friday that "there's a lot of questions about Hegseth."

"We have no idea what the strategy is moving forward in Iran. No one's happy about Iran," Comer told NewsNation .

When Democrats take control of both the House and Senate next year, they will have the ability to call for hearings and launch investigations into virtually any aspect of the Trump administration — and Hegseth's handling of the military is high on their list.

"In the majority, one of the first things we're gonna do is run Pete Hegseth out of town," Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the minority leader who is poised to become House speaker in January, said at a rally last month .

Rep. Thomas Massie, a Republican from Kentucky and vocal Trump critic, said he intends to force a House vote on articles of impeachment against Hegseth as soon as next week, citing violations of the War Powers Resolution, bypassing Congress on war declarations and unlawful military actions in several countries.

Massie — who in May lost his bid for reelection to Ed Gallrein, a Trump-backed challenger, in the Republican primary — introduced articles of impeachment against Hegseth in September. But House Speaker Mike Johnson later canceled the final scheduled voting day before the midterm recess, delaying a vote.

In a post on X Wednesday , Massie wrote that "there is one contingency in which I won't reintroduce the articles of impeachment: Hegseth resigns."

In a 5-and-a-half-minute video posted to X on Thursday afternoon, Hegseth defended the Iran war, touted changes he's implemented as Pentagon chief ("We ended the weird and the woke") and praised Trump's leadership while dismissing Massie's impeachment pursuit.

"A disgruntled, defeated congressman along with all his Democrat allies has dropped sham impeachment articles against yours truly," Hegseth said. "It didn't work with President Trump and it won't work with me."

Tillis responded on X. "Cabinet secretaries shouldn't be wasting taxpayer dollars on campaign style videos," he wrote, adding that the issue was "the incompetence you've displayed" and "the bad advice you've given to president."

articles.title: US offers $20m reward for information about Iran's nuclear programme
articles.summary: Donald Trump has repeatedly raised the prospecting of renewing strikes against Iran's nuclear facilities.
articles.body:
The US has announced a reward of up to $20 million for information about Iran's nuclear programme.

The State Department's Rewards for Justice is also offering to potentially relocate the person who provides such details.

President Donald Trump claimed last year that Iran's nuclear facilities had been "completely and totally obliterated " following a bombing campaign by the US and Israel.

Iran insists its nuclear programme is peaceful and that it has no intention of developing a nuclear weapon.

Meanwhile, the US military says it is setting up a task force to enhance Washington's efforts to restrict Iran's movement of weapons and sanctioned material across its borders.

The US military's Central Command (Centcom) said Task Force Iron Gate would operate from Tampa, Florida, and would work with other US government agencies.

As well as the movement of weapons, it will also focus on dual-use and illegal revenue streams.

Centcom estimates that its naval blockade of Iran's ports has prevented the country from exporting more than $25bn in crude oil.

Major construction ongoing near Iran missile bases, satellite images suggest

A US State Department statement about its multi-million dollar reward said it was offering the money for information about the Iranian programme, including "facilities, equipment and associated personnel".

It said Iran's "lack of compliance with the IAEA [the International Atomic Energy Agency] on safeguards obligations has led to the agency's loss of 'continuity of knowledge' regarding Iran's production and inventory of key components like [nuclear] centrifuges".

Centrifuges are needed to produce enriched uranium, which can be used to make reactor fuel for civilian use but also for nuclear weapons if enriched to around 90% purity or higher.

There had been mounting speculation that the US might resume significant strikes in Iran after the midterm elections, though Trump told reporters, prior to the polls, that he was in "no rush" to do so.

In an interview with Fox News on the eve of the midterms, the president also said the US "might need to go after Pickaxe [Mountain]", an underground site linked to Iran's nuclear programme.

This was "not a big deal" and could be done in "one hour", Trump said.

The president has repeatedly threatened to bomb the suspected underground site on previous occasions.

However, both Trump and Vice-President JD Vance have said public opposition to the war on Iran fuelled heavy losses for their Republican Party in this week's midterm elections, which has led to speculation the White House may no longer seek an escalation in the conflict.

On Friday, Trump insisted that Iran was keen to end the eight-month conflict with the US, stressing the damage to Tehran's economy and military.

"We're dealing with them now. They want to make a deal very badly," he said.

Qatar's foreign ministry spokesman said on Tuesday that both sides were "reviewing the ideas and proposals we have presented" and that it remained hopeful of a deal being agreed.

Iranian negotiators had discussed with mediators a proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days once the US met its seven conditions.

The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.
