articles.title: Meet Stephen Miller, Trump’s new chief of staff: 5 things to know
articles.summary: President Trump announced Friday that longtime White House aide Stephen Miller would be his next chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles — who has served in the role since Trump returned to office. Miller is an immigration hardliner and Trump loyalist who has been with the president since he launched his first campaign. The promotion…
articles.body:
President Trump announced Friday that longtime White House aide Stephen Miller would be his next chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles — who has served in the role since Trump returned to office.

Miller is an immigration hardliner and Trump loyalist who has been with the president since he launched his first campaign. The promotion was highly controversial among Democrats and even some Republicans, who see Miller as partly responsible for the GOP’s midterm losses, when the part lost control of the House and Senate and Democrats won large majorities.

Here are five things to know about Stephen Miller.

Miller started his career in Washington working as a press secretary for Rep. Michele Bachmann (R-Minn) in 2007 and later for Rep. John Shadegg (R-Ariz.). In 2009, he served as Alabama Sen. Jeff Sessions’s press secretary before moving up the ranks — becoming his communications chief.

Miller pushed Sessions to become more outspoken and combative, especially on the issue of immigration. He helped Sessions kill a bipartisan immigration reform bill in 2013 by writing a handbook to help lawmakers defeat it.

Behind the scenes, Miller carved out an inside-the-Beltway reputation as a hard-charging press aide, frequently battling with reporters and others in Washington.

When Trump announced his run for the presidency in 2015, Sessions became the first senator to endorse him. The Alabama senator went onto to serve as the president’s attorney general during his first stint in the White House.

But Sessions eventually fell out with Trump after recusing himself from investigations into Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign and election win.

Miller, in contrast, became a part of Trump’s inner circle and was a confidant to the president for the rest of his first term, his years out of office and during his second term.

Miller is considered the architect behind much of Trump’s immigration policies — most recently his administration’s mass deportation efforts.

As deputy chief of staff for policy, Miller pushed the administration to suspend habeas corpus rights, which allow people in custody to challenge their detention, and triple its daily immigration arrest goals to 3,000.

One of the administration’s most high-profile immigration blitzes in Trump’s second term was “Operation Metro Surge” in Minneapolis, during which federal agents fatally shot two American citizens. Miller at the time called both victims “domestic terrorists.”

In the first Trump administration, Miller was also a primary advocate of the administration’s family separation policy.

Before his promotion to chief of staff, Miller was already in the president’s ear as a key policy adviser. He will now be one of the top voices in the Trump White House and among other influential people in Washington.

Miller is one of the only aides from Trump’s first term to be serving in a high role in his second term. He has a deep understanding of how Washington runs, and is known to dig deep into policy matters. His background as a Senate aide gives him a strong understanding of how Congress works, and on how executive authority can be used to assert presidential power.

During debates over legislation affecting immigration, Miller was seen as having a big influence on the stance Republicans took. He is known as a detail-oriented aide who reads briefs, asks questions and demands results.

As chief of staff, Miller will be able to have his fingers on everything the White House touches. Wiles, the outgoing chief, was seen by some as a brake on Miller. With her gone, that brake would be lost just as Miller takes what has histocially been seen as the second most powerful role at the White House, behind only the president himself.

The chief of staff works closely with the president on day-to-day operations and manages the White House staff. It can be a gatekeeper role for how sees the president and can be a position involved in all policy decisions, depending on the individual chief of staff.

It is a role that does not require Senate confirmation.

Miller’s wife, Katie Miller — a GOP political adviser and podcaster — has also established herself during Trump’s time in office and is well-connected in Republican circles. During the first term, she served as communications director and press secretary to then Vice President Pence.

When Trump returned to office, Katie Miller became an adviser to the controversial Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), an Elon Musk-led initiative to slash government spending and reduce the size of the workforce.

Katie Miller now hosts a podcast , “The Katie Miller Podcast,” directed at conservative women.

Many in the president’s orbit have come and gone over the past decade — including Wiles, who had a brief falling out with Trump before returning to run his campaign in 2024.

But Miller has remained loyal the entire time, from the 2016 campaign to both his terms in the White House.

When Trump lost reelection in 2020, Miller co-founded America First Legal , a conservative nonprofit advocating for dismantling diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) programs, enforcing immigration laws and protecting election integrity.

Miller rejoined Trump’s 2024 campaign and returned to the White House right away as deputy chief of staff for policy and an adviser on homeland security.

While most of the criticism around Miller’s promotion came from Democrats, some Republicans questioned whether Trump was making the right choice in light of sweeping midterm losses.

No critic of Miller in the GOP is louder than Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), who told the president to “rethink” his decision to promote the deputy chief. The North Carolina Republican has repeatedly criticized Miller’s immigration stance and accused him of giving the president bad advice.

“It is a colossal mistake, and the last thing we need 72 hours after the a– whooping we got on Tuesday,” Tillis told CNN Friday.

Even some former Trump administration officials questioned the move.

Sarah Matthews, a former deputy White House press secretary, called the notion of replacing Wiles with Miller “terrifying.”

Another former Trump administration official told The Hill Miller’s promotion is “exactly the opposite” direction from what voters demanded.

“It’s exactly the opposite direction voters are begging Republicans to go. Susie was the best thing that happened to President Trump,” the official said.

A former Trump chief of staff said choosing Miller is not likely to help the president forge a working relationship with the new Democratic majority.

articles.title: Biden-appointed judge probes whether ICE skirted judge's release orders in Colorado cases
articles.summary: Denver ICE field office director Nathan Rasper must appear in court after 14 detainees were re-arrested following court-ordered releases in Colorado.
articles.body: A Biden-appointed federal judge ordered ICE's Denver field office director to appear in court Monday amid concerns that immigration authorities violated judicial release orders by immediately re-arresting detainees, including at least one instance outside a detention facility. Nathan Rasper has been summoned as part of an inquiry involving 14 people who were re-arrested after being released from immigration detention. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) maintains that ICE complied with lawful court orders and that a judicial release order does not permanently shield individuals from immigration enforcement. "When an illegal alien is ordered released by a judge, that does not immunize the alien from immigration enforcement for all time," DHS said in a statement to Fox News Digital. "ICE may seek to re-arrest the alien in a way that complies with the judicial decision. To suggest that ICE cannot do this is nothing short of sabotage." The Nov. 5 order issued by U.S. District Judge Charlotte Sweeney followed an earlier ruling requiring the government to identify every case in Colorado since Oct. 27 in which ICE re-detained someone within 12 hours of a court-ordered release. Federal officials subsequently identified 14 petitioners who had been re-arrested after being released, but the filing did not provide the precise timing of when the re-arrests occurred. She directed officials to provide the exact dates and times of those releases and re-arrests and identify any additional individuals immediately detained following court-ordered releases. OBAMA, BIDEN JUDGES DRAW FRESH FIRE AS TRUMP’S IMMIGRATION COURT CLASHES HEAT UP: ‘ALMOST IMPOSSIBLE’ The additional reporting requirements followed a Nov. 4 hearing in which Sweeney questioned whether ICE was circumventing judicial orders by briefly releasing detainees before immediately taking them back into custody. At that hearing, she ordered Rasper to appear at a follow-up hearing Monday to address the agency's practices. The inquiry stems in part from the case of Ramon Quintero Alvarez, who was released from immigration detention on Oct. 27 before ICE immediately took him back into custody, according to a government court filing. In a Nov. 3 court filing, federal government attorneys said they would not submit a legal brief defending the lawfulness of Alvarez's continued detention. The filing prompted Sweeney to convene the Nov. 4 hearing at which Assistant U.S. Attorneys Andrew Soler and Kevin Traskos appeared alongside ICE Assistant Field Office Director Nichole Black, who testified under oath about the circumstances surrounding Alvarez's re-arrest. APPEALS COURT BLOCKS TRUMP ADMIN FROM HOLDING MIGRANTS WITHOUT BOND FOR OVER 90 DAYS At a Nov. 4 hearing, Sweeney ordered Alvarez be released and barred immigration authorities from detaining him again unless the government demonstrated, by clear and convincing evidence at a bond hearing, that he posed a flight risk or danger to the community. The government must submit the additional information requested by Sweeney by 8 a.m. Monday, ahead of Rasper's scheduled court appearance later that morning. The proceedings could shed light on ICE's compliance with judicial release orders, but Sweeney has not indicated whether she intends to pursue contempt proceedings. The dispute comes as ICE faces similar legal challenges across Colorado, where other Biden-appointed federal judges, including U.S. District Judges Nina Wang and S. Kato Crews, have presided over cases involving disputes over immigration detention and court-ordered releases. articles.title: Trump orders DOJ probe into Democrats over alleged threats against admin officials
articles.summary: President Donald Trump accused Democrats of threatening administration officials and Republican donors, ordering the DOJ to investigate alleged "criminal" conduct.
articles.body: President Donald Trump said he has ordered the Department of Justice to open an investigation into instances of Democratic lawmakers "threatening" to impeach Attorney General Todd Blanche, among others. The announcement, which was made via a Truth Social post Saturday afternoon, came after the Democrats retook control of the House and Senate in the midterm elections, winning strong majorities in both chambers of Congress. "The Democrats are going around threatening a lot of people, including the Attorney General of the United States, and others, with Impeachment and many other forms of punishment, even though they admit they have no reason to do so," Trump wrote. Since Election Day, two House Democrats — Reps. Hank Johnson, D-Ga., and Deborah Ross, D-N.C. — have publicly said they would support impeaching Blanche. HOUSE GOP ERUPTS AT STEPHEN MILLER AS TRUMP ELEVATES HIM AFTER MIDTERM MASSACRE: 'MEGALOMANIAC' "I personally believe that the offenses of Todd Blanche demand that he be impeached and convicted and removed from office," Johnson said Thursday in an interview on SiriusXM’s "The Dan Abrams Show." Ross went on host Dan Abrams' radio show shortly after Johnson and said she supported impeaching Blanche as well, but thought Democrats "should start with Hegseth." In his post, Trump denied that any "impeachable acts" had been committed by Blanche or any other administration officials. He didn't mention Johnson or Ross by name, nor did he mention the fact that Thomas Massie, R-Ky., will likely reintroduce impeachment articles against Secretary of War Pete Hegseth on Monday. Trump named only one Democratic politician, Sen. Elissa Slotkin of Michigan, in his post. He accused her of saying she would "go after all young people that believe in Republican Values." TRUMP CALLS OUT SENATE REPUBLICANS AFTER MIDTERM LOSSES Trump appears to have been referring to comments Slotkin made on Oct. 13 at the University of Chicago about wanting to pursue "signature cases" against people who "enabled" Trump. "I want young people coming out of school to say, 'Should I go work for the Trump administration? Like, that sounds fun, I might get an opportunity.' I want them to be like, 'Lord, that might be buying myself a ton of problems that I don't want, and so let me avoid participating in that,'" Slotkin said. "I want that deterrence message sent." Trump also said that Democrats have been threatening Republican donors "with imprisonment" because of their views. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The president did not identify the donors that have allegedly been threatened. Democrats have, however, signaled they plan to investigate some major Republican donors and corporations when they assume control of Congress, Reuters reported this week. This could include donors to the White House ballroom. Trump concluded his post by saying "these EXTORTIONISTS" should be imprisoned and that he wanted the DOJ to investigate the alleged actions as a "criminal act."

articles.body:
President Trump said he offered the job of White House press secretary to Dana White, president and CEO of the Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC).

In a Truth Social post Saturday, Trump said he requested White bring “assistants” with him and named several UFC fighters.

“I am pleased to announce that the Great Dana White, a violent Fighter and Warrior, has been offered the job of Press Secretary of the United States,” Trump wrote. “I have requested that he bring with him assistants, even though some are not from our Country, of Islam Makhachev, Khabib Nurmagomedov, Justin Gaethje, Daniel Cormier, Amanda Nunes, and Kayla Harris.”

“We need these people to defend us against the Lunatic Left. Dana will be a Press Secretary like none other. Dana, please take the job!” he added.

It is unclear whether White has accepted the position, though the UFC president shared an image of himself at the White House press briefing room podium to his Instagram story with the caption, “On to the next chapter” — a post which came shortly after Trump’s announcement. White followed up the image with another story post, a screenshot of the president’s statement.

White House-affiliated account Rapid Response 47 also posted a screenshot to social platform X of Trump’s Truth Social post.

The White House did not immediately respond to The Hill’s request to confirm the offer.

Trump and White have had a close relationship in recent years. White’s UFC hosted a fight on the White House South Lawn over the summer, part of the ongoing celebrations for America’s 250th anniversary. The CEO of UFC’s parent company, Andrew Schleimer, said it lost $30 million on the White House fight.

The attendance at the fight illustrated Trump’s cozy relationship with business leaders. Those attending the White House fight, which was broadcast exclusively on Paramount+, included Paramount CEO David Ellison and Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, among other high-profile guests.

The White House has been searching for a permanent press secretary after the departure of Karoline Leavitt earlier this year. Trump briefly tapped political commentator Katie Zacharia for the job, but she was dismissed after less than a week in the role and only one short press briefing. Zacharia left the post after reports emerged that she had marketed herself as an attorney without passing the bar exam.

White would be an unconventional choice for Trump, though many in the president’s orbit did not come from political backgrounds before being nominated.

articles.title: Bill Maher warns Democrats that some on far-left want 'communism' after midterm sweep
articles.summary: Bill Maher told his "Real Time" audience that far-left Democrats "want communism" and urged moderates to use their midterm wins to reclaim the party.
articles.body:
Comedian Bill Maher doubled down on his criticism of democratic socialists Friday, telling his "Real Time" audience that "these people want communism" and urging moderates to reclaim control of the party following Democrats' historic sweep in this week's midterm elections.

On Friday, Maher spoke with writer and podcast host Coleman Hughes regarding the rise of socialist policies within the Democratic Party — and the party's apparent appetite for more moderate candidates — during the show's roundtable discussion.

"My issues are high rents and crime," Hughes said. "Socialists don't tend to be good on those issues because they institute policies like rent control, which sound good and then end up increasing the rents in the long run."

"And we got a hundred years of data on socialism ," Hughes added. "It's not good for the economy. It's not a new idea."

Maher appeared to agree with his guest, arguing that many of the policies pushed by socialist candidates are more closely aligned with communist ideology.

"We already have a lot of socialism and a lot of it is appropriate," Maher said. "That's not what these people are selling, these far-left people."

Maher said some government services and programs — including Medicare, the Marine Corps and Social Security — fall under his definition of socialism.

"It's anything the government does and the private sector doesn't," the comedian said. "You just read what they say in their manifesto. They want the government to take over everything. That is a prescription for failure."

Maher also argued that the sweeping victories by moderate Democrats could indicate a broader voter rejection of the policies advocated by far-left candidates.

"To me, one of the great results of this election was it gave moderates a big stick to beat them off with," Maher told his audience.

He added that moderate Democrats could use their midterm victories to regain control of the party, while suggesting that the socialist agenda may not be as popular with voters as its supporters believe.

"Who has the guts to say this is the Democratic Party, you are doing a whole different thing," he continued. "We already have a lot of socialism, and I'm for most of it. We need most of it, but these people want communism."

The liberal comedian has repeatedly criticized the rise of socialism within the Democratic Party and warned about socialist policies ahead of the midterms earlier this year.

"I did say that it was about two months ago, and you see how quickly the news changes in just two months, because that was before the Supreme Court made a ruling on voting rights," Maher said at an event in June, referencing the Supreme Court's April 29 decision in "Louisiana v. Callais," which found that Louisiana's revised congressional map constituted an unconstitutional racial gerrymander.

"So, that has changed just in the last two months, and then the Democrats just elected three very far-left democratic socialists in New York who are crazy — like outright really crazy — so like, how are they gonna blow it? I don't know, but they seem to be well on their way," he added at the time.

Maher's comments come after Democrats have won at least 254 U.S. House of Representatives races, according to the Associated Press — subsequently giving the party its largest House majority since 2009 .

Additionally, democratic socialist Nithya Raman defeated incumbent Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass earlier this week, becoming another democratic socialist elected to lead a major American city, following New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani's victory last year.

However, Democratic strategist Kaivan Shroff told Fox News Digital that Maher's criticisms of socialist policies — and his characterization of candidates who support them — are misguided as the comedian continues to criticize Democrats.

"There is something perfectly 'Bill Maher' about declaring it an 'indictment of our educational system' that young people supposedly do not understand socialism, and then immediately revealing that he does not understand it either," Shroff said. "Medicare and Social Security are social insurance programs. The Marine Corps is literally a branch of the military."

"If every service the government provides counts as socialism, then courts, cops and Congress are socialist too and the word has basically lost all meaning," he added. "He is mocking other people for being uneducated on the subject while demonstrating the same sloppy understanding himself."

Shroff also pointed to Maher's history of dining with President Donald Trump at the White House — most recently last month — and accused the liberal comedian of criticizing socialist policies more harshly when Democrats embrace them.

"And if Maher really wants to worry about socialism, he might want to look a little harder at his dinner buddy Donald Trump," Shroff said. "Trump's government has taken roughly a 10 percent stake in Intel and about a 15 percent stake in MP Materials. Those examples are far closer to socialism than Medicare is. Yet somehow Maher's socialism panic gets a lot quieter when Trump is the one doing it."

Fox News Digital reached out to Maher for comment.

Fox News Digital's Peter D'Abrosca contributed to this report.

articles.title: How did AIPAC-backed candidates fare in the US midterm elections?
articles.summary: Many candidates the pro-Israel group backed still won, but most of the money it spent went to candidates who lost.
articles.body:
Nearly a year before he stunned many by winning a seat in the United States Senate from Texas, James Talarico drew attention for his vehement rejection of campaign funding from the country’s largest pro-Israel lobbying group, the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC).

“I’ve never taken money from AIPAC, and I’m not taking money from AIPAC in this campaign,” Talarico said in a clip for a podcast that later went viral. “Seeing what’s happening in Gaza makes me sick to my stomach as a teacher, as a Christian, as a human being.”

On November 3, Talarico won by more than 12 percentage points. Pro-Israel groups allied with AIPAC gave modest support – about $6,000 – to Talarico’s opponent, Ken Paxton, but Talarico’s willingness to be so open about his disdain for AIPAC is still a notable part of a shift in US politics.

In races across the country, AIPAC and political spending groups linked to it poured tens of millions of dollars into backing one candidate or another. While the group did back many winning candidates, nearly two-thirds of the total money it spent this election cycle went to those who ended up losing.

Even among Republicans, candidates are thinking twice about taking funds from the group, said Rina Shah, a geopolitical adviser and strategist and a former senior GOP congressional aide.

“A few years ago, taking AIPAC support was a no-brainer for most GOP candidates,” she told Al Jazeera. “Now, with a younger, more America First wing asking hard questions about foreign entanglements, and Gaza weighing on voters across the spectrum, it’s become a real topic, not a niche one.”

How AIPAC spends money has become more opaque . In October, for instance, the group said it would stop endorsing candidates and making direct contributions to them after this election cycle. Much of its spending already runs through affiliated political action committees, such as its super PAC, the United Democracy Project (UDP), making donations harder to track.

AIPAC has funded hundreds of candidates in the midterm elections, in both primaries and the general election on November 3, according to Track AIPAC, an organisation that records the group’s funding of US politicians. The organisation tabulates spending by UDP as well as nearly 50 other PACs tied to the pro-Israel lobbying group.

On November 4, the day after the Democratic Party roundly defeated Republicans and won control of both the House and Senate, AIPAC said it had already counted some 234 candidates it backed, from both parties, as having won their contests.

Candidates won, but most money went to waste

In terms of the number of winning candidates, the group still has a strong record. Pro-Israel groups like AIPAC and UDP backed candidates in at least 32 of 35 Senate races this election, according to Track AIPAC. In 26 of those races, the groups spent more than $100,000 on a candidate, and 21 of those candidates won their races on November 3.

“AIPAC members are determined to expand their political activism in the cycles ahead,” the group said in a post on X that specifically pointed to support for the two most powerful Democrats in Congress – Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries – who have also continued to call for maintaining strong US ties with Israel.

But nearly two-thirds of the total money pro-Israel groups spent in the midterm elections went to candidates who lost, according to a tally by the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft. Around $55m of the $84m that AIPAC, UDP and linked groups spent in the election cycle went to candidates who did not win, according to the findings.

“We have entered a new era,” said Trita Parsi, executive vice president of the Quincy Institute, a foreign policy think tank that advocates for less US foreign involvement. “It is not just that AIPAC is spending millions of dollars and losing. You also have a new reality now in which candidates find AIPAC’s donations toxic and are rejecting it.”

The most notable race in which an AIPAC-backed candidate lost was for a Senate seat in Michigan, where the group and affiliated PACs spent some $30m on Representative Haley Stevens, a Democrat who unsuccessfully sought the party’s nomination for the contest. According to the New York Times, AIPAC then poured an additional $9m into backing Republican Mike Rogers, who lost on November 3 to Abdul El-Sayed, an outspoken critic of Israel who has called for the US to stop giving financial support to the country.

“Thank you for giving me the opportunity to beat you twice,” El-Sayed said in his victory speech on election night, addressing the pro-Israel lobbying group.

In Maine, AIPAC-linked groups gave more than $4.8m in support of Senator Susan Collins’s re-election campaign. Collins lost to Democrat Troy Jackson, who flipped a seat long held by Republicans.

In California, Melissa Hernandez received more than $6m in backing from UDP and other pro-Israel groups this year, as she sought to defeat Aisha Wahab, a left-leaning Afghan American who has frequently been critical of Israel , in a contest for a seat in the House. Wahab won that race.

Backing candidates who won again in Democratic strongholds

But in other races, the pro-Israel groups have successfully backed candidates, especially in primary races in recent years, ensuring that the Democratic Party ends up nominating candidates who are not too far to the left and not overly critical of Israel.

In Missouri, AIPAC-related groups provided more than about $3m in funding to support Representative Wesley Bell. Bell, a Democrat running in a traditional stronghold for the party, won a seat in the House on November 3 with more than 81 percent of the vote. Most of that money was spent in primaries, where AIPAC financially backed Bell’s campaign against former Representative Cori Bush, who was one of the first lawmakers in Congress to call Israel’s war on Gaza a genocide and who had lost to Bell in a primary in 2024. Previously, AIPAC-related groups funneled $8m into beating Bush that year. Jeffries supported Bell in this year’s primary rematch.

In another Democratic win in a party stronghold, George Latimer was re-elected to the House to represent a New York district just north of New York City. AIPAC spent some $14m defeating his opponent in 2024, when he ousted left-wing Israel critic Jamaal Bowman.

UDP also spent more than $4m in 2024 on another primary, this time helping Democrat Sarah Elfreth beat out more left-leaning candidates to win the party’s nomination. Elfreth again won in the heavily Democratic district on November 3.

Not the only lobbying group on Israel in town

AIPAC is no longer the only lobbying group on Israel, though.

J Street , a Jewish American group that describes itself as pro-Israel and pro-peace, said on November 4 that it had backed more than 200 candidates with more than $13m in funding, in a campaign aimed especially at candidates backed by AIPAC.

It has especially sought to back Democratic candidates who offer a more moderate view on Israel, even as some party leaders have claimed that being more overtly critical of Israel would alienate Jewish voters. But a poll commissioned by J Street found that 72 percent of American Jewish voters still backed the party in the midterm elections.

“In an election with so much at stake for American democracy, we are proud to have supported a record number of candidates who share our commitment to Israel’s future, democracy and a peaceful resolution to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict,” J Street President Jeremy Ben-Ami said in a statement.

articles.title: STU BURGUIERE: Put your money where your mouth is: Prediction markets won the midterms
articles.summary: Billions of dollars in political advertising tried to mislead voters, but Kalshi's prediction markets had winners ahead in 98% of federal races.
articles.body: Billions of dollars were spent this election season to lie to you. More than $12.8 billion was spent on political advertising in the 2026 midterms making this the most expensive election cycle in American history. In my home state of Texas, the Senate race drew preliminary estimates of nearly $573 million placing it among the most expensive non-presidential contests on record. Despite all the differences between races and candidates, a few things were dependable. Every campaign said it was going to win. Every analyst said their numbers were right. Every super PAC said its candidate had the best policies and character. And the mainstream media picked its favorites, cut to commercial, and served up a dozen ads of warring politicians accusing each other of high crimes and misdemeanors. TRADERS POUR NEARLY $1.3 BILLION INTO PREDICTING WHO WILL CONTROL CONGRESS A massive industry exists to bend your view of reality toward whatever our would-be leaders in Washington and the state capitals want you to believe. Americans need a way to cut through that noise. No wonder prediction markets are booming. How did prediction markets do on Election Day? As with any new technology, prediction markets have drawn a lot of attention and a lot of criticism. Senators wrote letters warning about election contracts. States moved to sue or ban them outright. And somewhere, a podcaster is still on hour 133 of explaining how it's all rigged. POLLSTERS MISSED THE MARK AGAIN — BUT THIS TIME, IT WASN'T REPUBLICANS THEY UNDERESTIMATED Then Election Day settled the argument. articles.title: Trump asks DOJ to investigate Democrats calling for impeachment of cabinet officials
articles.summary: President Trump raised concerns Saturday about some Democrats calling for the impeachment of Republican officials, referring to the threats as “extortion at the highest level” and asking the Justice Department to “look into this.” “The Democrats are going around threatening a lot of people … with Impeachment and many other forms of punishment, even though…
articles.body:
President Trump raised concerns Saturday about some Democrats calling for the impeachment of Republican officials, referring to the threats as “extortion at the highest level” and asking the Justice Department to “look into this.”

“The Democrats are going around threatening a lot of people … with Impeachment and many other forms of punishment, even though they admit they have no reason to do so, and there have been no impeachable acts committed, or even thought of, by the victims of this illegal process,” the president wrote in a Truth Social post Saturday.

“This is extortion at the highest level, and they should be held accountable for this,” he added.

Just two days after Election Day, two House Democrats voiced their support of impeaching GOP officials like Attorney General Todd Blanche and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. This came shortly after Democrats seized control of the House and the Senate after winning tough races in battleground states like Texas, Michigan, Maine, Kansas, Iowa and Ohio.

Rep. Hank Johnson (D-Ga.), in an interview with SiriusXM’s “The Dan Abrams Show,” said Thursday, “I personally believe that the offenses of Todd Blanche demand that he be impeached and convicted and removed from office.”

Fellow Democratic Rep. Deborah Ross (N.C.), who also appeared on the show, echoed Johnson’s statement — noting she thinks removing Hegseth should be a top priority.

But calls for Hegseth’s impeachment came from both sides of the aisle, with Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) telling CNN he plans to call for a vote to impeach the defense secretary.

In Wednesday night post on social platform X , Massie said, “There is one contingency in which I won’t reintroduce the articles of impeachment: Hegseth resigns.”

In another post the following day, the Kentucky Republican said his impeachment resolution is “ a much gentler version of what’s coming when Dem’s control Congress. They’ll have hearings & trials.”

Hegseth responded to the impeachment threats Thursday in a video posted to X, in which he said, “A disgruntled, defeated congressman, along with all his Democrat allies, has also dropped sham articles of impeachment against yours truly.”

“This is Weaponization and Lawfare at another level,” Trump said in his Saturday post.

“I am ordering the Department of Justice to look into this criminal act, immediately!,” he added.

articles.title: Republican Kris Kobach loses AG reelection bid in Kansas

Kobach lost to Chris Mann, a former prosecutor and police officer who nearly beat him in 2024. Mann leads with 50.6 percent of the vote to Kobach’s 49.4 percent, or a lead of…
articles.body:
Kansas Attorney General Kris Kobach has lost reelection, the Associated Press projected, denying him a second term as the state’s top lawyer.

Kobach lost to Chris Mann, a former prosecutor and police officer who nearly beat him in 2024. Mann leads with 50.6 percent of the vote to Kobach’s 49.4 percent, or a lead of about 13,000 votes. Decision Desk HQ, The Hill’s election desk partner, has not yet called the race.

The Sunflower State attorney general is best known for his accusations of widespread election fraud, including while he was Kansas secretary of state, the top election official. He was the vice chair of President Trump’s voter fraud commission in his first term, a task force that aimed to find the “full truth” about voter fraud in U.S. elections.

The commission drew controversy for demanding states turn over voter roll information that included partial Social Security numbers — a move that received pushback from both parties. Kobach then said Kansas would not hand over the last four digits of voters’ Social Security numbers despite his commission making that request of other states.

A report from Maine’s then-Secretary of State Matt Dunlap showed that the commission did not find any widespread voter fraud. Trump dissolved the commission.

Kobach’s loss is his second statewide defeat in a general election in the past 10 years, despite Kansas typically being a deep-red state.

Gov. Laura Kelly (D) defeated Kobach in the 2018 gubernatorial race by a seven-point margin. He later ran in the GOP primary for U.S. Senate in 2020, but lost to now-Sen. Roger Marshall.

Kobach’s Tuesday defeat was one of many for Kansas Republicans, led by Democrat Adam Hamilton’s victory in the Senate race. The Methodist pastor defeated Marshall by five points and became the first Democrat to win a U.S. Senate seat in Kansas in nearly 100 years.

Kansas Democrats are also poised to pick up 20 seats in the state House with nearly all votes counted. The party appears likely to hold the governor’s mansion, though a winner has not been projected.

Inroads in Kansas were part of a Democratic surge nationally. The party flipped Senate seats in red states like Texas, South Carolina, Iowa and Ohio and won several gubernatorial races in states that currently have Republican governors.

articles.title: Trump orders DOJ to look into Democrats for 'threatening' people
articles.summary: WASHINGTON, Nov 7 () - President Donald Trump ordered the US Justice Department on Saturday to look into Democrats for "threatening a lot of people" with imp...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON, Nov 7 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump ordered the US Justice Department on Saturday to look into Democrats for "threatening a lot of people" with impeachment and other ‌forms of punishment, saying in a social media post that their actions amount to a "criminal ‌act," without providing evidence.

Democratic candidates routed Trump's Republicans in midterm elections on Tuesday, giving them control of Congress starting ​in January. Party leaders have promised to reassert Congress' oversight of the executive branch once they are in power by holding hearings and conducting investigations into Trump administration actions.

In his post, Trump accused Democrats of sending "threatening letters to many people, all innocent."

Members of Congress have released copies of letters seeking documents ‌on matters such as tech company ⁠donations for the large ballroom Trump is building at the White House.

Trump's post also referred to Democratic Senator Elissa Slotkin of Michigan, who suggested in remarks ⁠last month at the University of Chicago that Congress should investigate people who have enabled Trump's policies.

"I want young people coming out of school to say, 'Should I go work for the Trump administration?' … I want ​them ​to be like, 'Lord, that might be buying myself a ​ton of problems that I don't want. ‌And so I might avoid participating in that,'" Slotkin said. "I want that deterrence message sent."

Her comments, within weeks of the midterm elections, were criticized by some Republicans. Republican Senator Mike Lee of Utah wrote on social media that Slotkin was threatening young people who wanted to go into politics. Slotkin responded that Lee had lied about her comments and wrote, "Spare us the manufactured outrage."

Trump's Justice ‌Department has investigated Slotkin before. A former CIA analyst, ​she was among a group of Democratic lawmakers with ​national security backgrounds whom the department investigated ​after they posted a video urging service members and intelligence officials to disobey ‌illegal orders from the administration.

A grand jury ​rejected the attempt to ​indict them.

Slotkin said in a social media post on Saturday that the issue should not be controversial. "If you break the law or use taxpayer dollars to enrich yourself, you should ​be held accountable. If you ‌didn't break the law, then it's all good," she said.

The Justice Department did not ​immediately respond to requests for comment.

(Reporting by Susan Heavey in Washington; Writing by Patricia ​Zengerle; Editing by Sergio Non and Cynthia Osterman)

articles.title: Rep.-elect Ojeda posts tribute to father who died after midterms: ‘He held on’
articles.summary: Democratic North Carolina Rep.-elect Richard Ojeda on Friday posted a tribute for his late father who passed away following the Democrat’s win in the midterm elections. “For years, my dad battled Parkinson’s disease. On Election Night, I got to tell him, “Pop, we won.” This morning, he passed away,” Ojeda wrote in post on social…
articles.body:
Democratic North Carolina Rep.-elect Richard Ojeda on Friday posted a tribute for his late father who passed away following the Democrat’s win in the midterm elections.

“For years, my dad battled Parkinson’s disease. On Election Night, I got to tell him, “Pop, we won.” This morning, he passed away,” Ojeda wrote in post on social platform X on Friday.

“A part of me believes he held on just long enough to see his son make it to Congress. He won’t be there when I’m sworn in. But I know he’ll be standing right beside me,” the newly elected congressman added.

Ojeda defeated Rep. Richard Hudson (R), the chair of the National Republican Congressional Committee (NRCC), in a close race for North Carolina’s 9th Congressional District which includes Hoke, Moore, Randolph and Alamance counties, along with portions of Guilford, Cumberland and Chatham counties.

The Democrat eked out a victory with more than 51 percent votes while the Republican incumbent secured a little less than 49 percent of the votes, according to Decision Desk HQ . His victory marks the first Democratic win in the district since 1963.

North Carolina’s flipped seat in the 9th Congressional District was in line with the Democrats’ sweeping victory in the midterm elections where they took control of both the House and the Senate, securing major wins in battleground states across the country.

In another post on Friday night on social platform X, said his father, “Richard Neece Ojeda lived an extraordinary life” and he “traveled the world and lived a life of service that started in the US Air Force and continued after graduating from the Mayo Clinic where he was commissioned as an officer in the US Army.”

He noted that his father spent 55 years after his military service practicing anesthesia and was the “first man in Logan County history to perform an epidural at Logan Regional Hospital in Logan, WV.”

In his morning post, Ojeda dedicated his Congressional victory to his father saying, “Rest easy, Daddy. I’ll take it from here. These next two years are for you.”

articles.title: Liberal podcasters apologize after laughing at joke about digging up Charlie Kirk's body
articles.summary: Jennifer Welch and Angie Sullivan laughed on the "I've Had It" podcast over a post referencing Charlie Kirk's death, sparking outrage.
articles.body: Podcasters Jennifer Welch and Angie Sullivan drew criticism from political commentators after laughing at a social media post about exhuming the body of conservative activist Charlie Kirk. The two issued an apology on Saturday. During Thursday's episode of Welch's "I've Had It" podcast, the two women laughed as they read social media reactions to Democrats' victories in the 2026 midterm elections. Several posts mocked conservative positions on issues including abortion, vaccines and LGBTQ+ policies. "Somebody posted, ‘I don’t care if you celibate or abstinent. Grab the nearest person available and do your worst. Abortion’s on me,’" Welch said, reading from the social media posts. STATE OF PLAY: BLUE WAVE SWEEPS DEMOCRATS INTO POWER, WITH KEY RACES STILL HANGING IN BALANCE The pair continued to laugh as they read other social media reactions mocking Republicans following the party's midterm election losses. "You can't even fathom the pronouns we're going to invent," Welch read while laughing. "You can't even pronounce them." The podcast host praised the writers of the various posts, calling the jokesters "patriots" and insisting that "these people make me patriotic." Welch further broke out into laughter while reading another post aloud: "We're digging up Charlie Kirk and doing it again." 'SNL' WEEKEND UPDATE ANCHOR CALLS REPUBLICANS SLURS, MOCKS CHARLIE KIRK IN STAND-UP SPECIAL On Saturday, the two hosts apologized via a post on Instagram. "On Thursday’s show, we laughed at a joke about Charlie Kirk. It was an insensitive joke, and we should not have laughed. We regret it, and we apologize," the statement read. "Whatever our political differences, there is nothing funny about gun violence. We’ve long supported common-sense gun safety reform." "To that end, we’ve made a donation to Everytown for Gun Safety, the largest gun violence prevention organization in America," the statement continued. "We’ll keep using our platforms to fight for the safety of all Americans." During Thursday's episode, after laughing at the post, the hosts said, "No comment," before asserting without presenting evidence that Tyler Robinson, the man accused of killing Kirk, supported President Donald Trump. DEMOCRATIC STUDENT GROUP TO PROTEST CHARLIE KIRK MEMORIAL AT CAMPUS WHERE HE WAS KILLED "Other than he was shot by somebody that was super MAGA," Sullivan said. "He was shot by a MAGA person," Welch said, adding, "White person, White MAGA family." REMEMBERING CHARLIE KIRK: TURNING POINT USA'S ANDREW KOLVET REFLECTS ON CONSERVATIVE GROUP'S CHALLENGING YEAR While Robinson and his family lived in Utah’s Washington County, a deep red county where 75% of residents voted to send President Donald Trump back to the White House, Fox News Digital previously reported that Utah Voter Registration records showed that Robinson is unaffiliated with a political party and did not vote in the past two general elections. Several commentators criticized the hosts' remarks on social media. PETE DAVIDSON SPARKS BACKLASH AFTER EXPLICIT JOKE ABOUT SLAIN CHARLIE KIRK DURING NETFLIX ROAST "In all of their hatred and blood thirst, these ghouls seriously consider themselves morally superior to you," conservative activist Riley Gaines said in an X post. "They will celebrate your death, laugh uncontrollably, and still be fully convinced they're the 'good guys,'" influencer Collin Rugg posted. Media Research Center President David Bozell also criticized the hosts, telling Fox News Digital, "If Madison Ave. would stop sponsoring gutter trash, gutter trash would go out of business." Democratic strategist Kaivan Shroff also criticized Welch and Sullivan's remarks. BOBBY BURACK: ONLINE HATE IS WINNING, FROM PAT MCAFEE TO EVERYDAY AMERICANS AND YOUNG CHILDREN "As a Democrat, it is frustrating to watch Jennifer Welch and Angie Sullivan get treated like voices for the Democratic Party when so much of their own brand is railing against Democrats," Shroff told Fox News Digital. "Have either of them persuaded a single person to vote for a Democrat?" "Then, after Democrats just delivered historic wins and a massive blue wave, they say something this offensive and irresponsible and suddenly the story is about them instead," he added. "They are not helping Democrats. They are hijacking the attention Democrats actually earned at the ballot box." articles.title: Melania Trump secures $7.2M for foster care scholarships at LSU ahead of Alabama showdown
articles.summary: Melania Trump unveiled a $7.2 million scholarship endowment at LSU for foster care youth before receiving a custom jersey and football tribute.
articles.body: BATON ROUGE, La. — First lady Melania Trump announced a $7.2 million scholarship endowment at Louisiana State University (LSU) on Saturday, delivering a message of hope to young Americans who have experienced foster care before receiving a special football tribute ahead of the Tigers' rivalry showdown against Alabama. Trump wore a Dalma suede bomber jacket by Nour Hammour, paired with an Adam Lippes skirt and Manolo Blahnik BB pumps for the occasion, blending her signature polished style with a more relaxed look suited to a college football weekend. The first lady's visit unfolded against a distinctly LSU backdrop, with purple-and-gold tailgating crowds lining the motorcade route and a massive American flag hanging above the stage inside Patrick F. Taylor Hall. LSU cheerleaders flanked Trump during her remarks, and the Tiger mascot presented her with both scholarship checks while wearing a signature "Be Best" T-shirt. MELANIA TRUMP CHALLENGES CONGRESS TO MAKE HER FOSTER CARE EXECUTIVE ORDER PERMANENT LAW: 'THEIR BIRTHRIGHT' There, university officials, donors and students gathered for an announcement supporting young Americans who have experienced foster care through Trump's "Fostering the Future" initiative. "This achievement will give young people from foster care an anchor of stability, a strong educational foundation, and a chance to build a wonderful life," Trump told attendees. The permanent endowment includes a $5 million commitment from MMR Group, led by LSU alumnus James B. "Pepper" Rutland, and an additional $2.2 million raised from 75 LSU Foundation donors. LSU Foundation President and CEO Krista Raney said the contributions had brought the scholarship fund to "more than $7.2 million and growing." LSU President Wade Rousse said the $5 million leadership gift is expected to generate approximately $200,000 annually, helping students cover tuition, fees, books and room and board. ED ORGERON-LANE KIFFIN PAIRING ALREADY PAYING DIVIDENDS FOR LSU TIGERS DURING PIVOTAL RECRUITING WEEKEND "At LSU, we believe talent is everywhere, but we understand that opportunity is not," Rousse said. The university also embraced the occasion with several football-themed gifts for the first lady. Trump received a custom purple-and-gold LSU jersey bearing the name "MELANIA" and the number 14, along with a Tigers helmet featuring her BE BEST Fostering the Future logo. Former LSU coach Ed Orgeron, known to fans as Coach O, joined the presentation with a specially designed commemorative football created by Big Game USA, a company owned by LSU alumnus Chris Calandra. The initiative extended beyond the ceremony, with special patches on LSU players' jerseys, helmet decals, cheerleader uniforms, mascot attire and commemorative fan towels, according to the White House. COLLEGE FOOTBALL'S FIRST FULL SATURDAY IS HERE AND IT'S A CELEBRATION OF AMERICA AT ITS BEST Southeastern Conference officials also agreed to use a special Melania Trump challenge coin for the game's official coin toss. The legendary LSU-Alabama rivalry even found its way into the scholarship announcement. After Trump revealed that LSU has 14 Fostering the Future scholars compared with Alabama's nine, Raney offered a lighthearted observation. "Mrs. Trump, what I heard you say is that LSU has 14 scholarship recipients and Alabama has nine," Raney said. "So I think that means we've already won the first point." Trump told attendees that 26 universities nationwide are supporting 100 Fostering the Future scholars this semester. "While most eyes will be on the athletes today, I encourage you to recognize LSU's Fostering the Future scholars, who are just as remarkable," she said. Louisiana Gov. Jeff Landry, Louisiana first lady Sharon Landry and House Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., were among those in attendance. Trump also received a handcrafted wooden bowl made from a fallen limb of one of LSU's historic oak trees, a gift symbolizing the lasting impact of the scholarship initiative. Fostering the Future, launched in 2021 as part of Trump's BE BEST initiative, seeks to expand educational opportunities for young people who have experienced foster care. She closed with an encouraging message to scholarship recipients. "To the Fostering the Future scholars here today, and throughout America: I see you. I believe in you. And I will keep working to create new opportunities with you," she said.

articles.title: Trump offers press secretary position to UFC head Dana White
articles.summary: President Donald Trump said that he’d offered the job of White House press secretary to the CEO and president of the Ultimate Fighting Championship, Dana White.
articles.body: President Donald Trump on Saturday said on Truth Social that he had offered the job of White House press secretary to Dana White, the CEO and president of the Ultimate Fighting Championship. “I am pleased to announce that the Great Dana White, a violent Fighter and Warrior, has been offered the job of Press Secretary of the United States,” the president wrote. Trump suggested in his post that White should bring several UFC fighters, including Khabib Nurmagomedov, Justin Gaethje and Amanda Nunes, as assistants to defend against the “Lunatic Left.” “Dana will be a Press Secretary like none other. Dana, please take the job!” he added. Trump and White have long been friends and the president has attended many UFC fights while serving in the White House. Earlier this year, White also organized a UFC fight on the South Lawn of the White House, an event that was part of a slate commemorating the United States’ 250th birthday. Many Trump administration officials and Republican lawmakers attended the fight in July. It’s unclear whether Trump’s offer to White to serve as press secretary is a serious one. A spokesperson for the White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The position has been vacant since Katie Zacharia departed the role after just five days in October. Zacharia had replaced Karoline Leavitt, who served as White House press secretary since Trump returned to office in January of last year. Leavitt announced in August that she would leave her post to spend more time with her family. The White House had another staff shake-up on Friday, when chief of staff Susie Wiles said she would be stepping down from her post. Trump named longtime aide Stephen Miller as her replacement.
